summary: Photosynthesis uses light energy to synthesise organic compounds and releases oxygen derived from water. Experiments establish its requirements; chloroplast membranes capture energy through photosystems, electron transport and chemiosmosis, while stromal reactions use ATP and NADPH to fix carbon. The Calvin cycle, C₄ carbon concentration, photorespiration and limiting factors together explain variation in photosynthetic efficiency and productivity.

items.content: The description of structure and variation of living organisms over a period of time, ended up as two, apparently irreconcilable perspectives on biology. The two perspectives essentially rested on two levels of organisation of life forms and phenomena. One described at organismic and above level of organisation while the second described at cellular and molecular level of organisation. The first resulted in ecology and related disciplines. The second resulted in physiology and biochemistry.
items.exam_note: Know the level-to-discipline associations. Avoid treating ecology and molecular explanations as mutually exclusive.

Connecting these scales prevents the mistaken idea that a molecular explanation and an ecological explanation must compete.

items.show: Zoom between the whole plant, its surroundings, cells and molecules.
items.level_extra: NEET distinction: organismic-and-above → ecology; cellular-and-molecular → physiology and biochemistry in this passage. These are perspectives, not mutually exclusive kinds of biology.

Cells form the structural and functional units of living organisms
Molecules are chemical components of cells

key_question.q: How can one plant make the connection between the two perspectives clear?
key_question.a: For the same plant, one can ask how environmental light affects its performance and then investigate light-driven reactions inside its cells. These are linked questions about one living system, viewed at different scales.

items.content: Description of physiological processes, in flowering plants as an example, is what is given in the chapters in this unit. The processes of photosynthesis, respiration and ultimately plant growth and development are described in molecular terms but in the context of cellular activities and even at organism level. Wherever appropriate, the relation of the physiological processes to environment is also discussed.
items.exam_note: Orientation rather than a detailed NEET mechanism. Do not infer that molecular description excludes cellular or environmental context.

why: To understand a living plant, we need more than the names of its parts: we must understand its activities.
The unit examines photosynthesis, respiration, growth and development in flowering plants through molecular explanations set within cellular and organismic activities.
Environmental relationships are added wherever appropriate, connecting internal activities with the conditions around the plant.

Light, water and air are parts of a plant's environment

key_question.q: Why should a molecular explanation still refer to the environment?
key_question.a: Plant processes operate under external conditions. For example, light availability influences photosynthesis, so understanding reactions inside cells also requires attention to conditions outside the plant.

key_question.a: Radiation emitted by a radioactive label can be detected, allowing researchers to follow labelled atoms. Its usefulness as a tracer does not mean that radio-activity is harmless.

key_question.a: Plants use light energy to produce organic matter. That matter can supply materials and can serve as an energy resource, linking photosynthetic production with both applications.

CHAPTER 11
PHOTOSYNTHESIS IN HIGHER PLANTS
items.exam_note: Chapter identification.

items.content: All animals including human beings depend on plants for their food. Have you ever wondered from where plants get their food? Green plants, in fact, have to make or rather synthesise the food they need and all other organisms depend on them for their needs. The green plants make or rather synthesise the food they need through photosynthesis and are therefore called autotrophs.
items.exam_note: Distinguish food synthesis from mineral absorption; autotroph does not mean an organism needs no external materials.

terms.meaning: छोटी चीज़ों को जोड़कर कोई चीज़ बनाना
terms.image: अलग सामान से रसोई में खाना बनना

terms.image: एक हरा पौधा, जिसे तैयार रोटी खिलानी नहीं पड़ती

why: Animals need food, so the opening puzzle asks who makes the food on which they depend.
Green plants synthesise their food through photosynthesis.
Food dependence extends from plants to plant-eaters and then to their consumers.
items.example: A green plant, a grazing animal and a human food chain.
items.leads_to: Plant food synthesis provides the starting point for understanding heterotrophic dependence.
items.show: Trace food from a green leaf to consumers.
items.level_extra: Auto means self; troph refers to nourishment. Separate organic food from water and mineral supplies.
needs_first: Animals obtain food by eating other organisms

key_question.q: How can an animal depend on plants even if it does not eat a plant directly?
key_question.a: A plant-eating animal obtains plant-made food, and a predator obtains that material and energy by eating the plant-eater. Dependence can therefore pass along a food chain.

items.content: You have already learnt that the autotrophic nutrition is found only in plants and all other organisms that depend on the green plants for food are heterotrophs.
items.exam_note: Do not infer that all non-plant organisms are heterotrophic; autotrophic bacteria are an important exception.

terms.meaning: जिन्हें food दूसरे organisms से मिलता है

terms.image: धूप में food बनाता हरा पौधा

Classify by nutritional ability, not merely by whether the organism is a plant or an animal.
items.example: A green leaf versus an animal feeding on plant-derived food.
items.leads_to: The nutritional distinction explains why photosynthesis matters beyond the plant.
items.show: Contrast making food with obtaining food.
items.level_extra: NEET trap: 'only plants are autotrophs' is not a universal biological statement.

key_question.q: Why must 'autotrophic nutrition is found only in plants' not be memorised as a universal rule?
key_question.a: Some bacteria are also autotrophic, including photosynthetic cyanobacteria and chemosynthetic bacteria. This page's plant-centred introduction is narrower than the biological distribution of autotrophy.

items.content: Green plants carry out ‘photosynthesis’, a physico-chemical process by which they use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds.
items.exam_note: Know the energy conversion: light energy to chemical energy. Do not confuse energy input with carbon input.

terms.meaning: light की energy लेकर organic food बनाना
terms.image: धूप पड़ती पत्ती में food बनने का दृश्य

Green plants use light energy to drive this synthesis.
The reactions connect light capture to chemical energy in food.
items.example: Photosynthesis in the green parts of an illuminated leaf.
items.leads_to: The definition sets up the later study of photosynthetic machinery and reactions.
items.show: Transform incoming light into chemical-energy storage.
items.level_extra: Distinguish conversion of energy from conversion of matter; sunlight is not the carbon source.

key_question.q: Why is the process called physico-chemical rather than just physical?
key_question.a: Light absorption is a physical interaction, but making organic substances involves chemical reactions. Light is an energy input, not a material ingredient that turns into sugar.

items.content: Ultimately, all living forms on earth depend on sunlight for energy. The use of energy from sunlight by plants doing photosynthesis is the basis of life on earth. Photosynthesis is important due to two reasons: it is the primary source of all food on earth. It is also responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere by green plants.
items.exam_note: Remember both roles: primary food production and oxygen release. Do not replace the second with carbon dioxide release.

terms.meaning: वह शुरुआती source जहाँ से food की supply शुरू होती है
terms.image: एक food chain की शुरुआत में हरा पौधा

Photosynthesis supplies plant-made food and releases oxygen into the atmosphere.
Food and oxygen together support the energy needs of aerobic consumers.
items.example: A green plant supplying plant-derived food to animals and oxygen to the surrounding air.
items.leads_to: Photosynthesis is an ecosystem-supporting process, not merely a way for a leaf to feed itself.
items.show: Branch plant output into food supply and atmospheric oxygen.
items.level_extra: Keep the two ecological roles distinct; the broader autotrophy exception is chemosynthesis.

key_question.q: What two reasons make photosynthesis important on this page?
key_question.a: It is described as the primary source of food on Earth and as the process responsible for oxygen release into the atmosphere by green plants.

items.content: Have you ever thought what would happen if there were no oxygen to breath [breathe]?
items.exam_note: Connect photosynthesis with aerobic respiration; do not claim that every organism requires oxygen.

key_question.q: How is breathing connected to food-derived energy?
key_question.a: Breathing supplies oxygen, which is used in aerobic cellular respiration; breathing itself is not the chemical breakdown of food.

items.content: This chapter focusses on the structure of the photosynthetic machinery and the various reactions that transform light energy into chemical energy.
items.exam_note: Orientation rather than a separate examinable mechanism.

terms.image: एक काम पूरा करने के लिए जुड़े हुए machine के parts

why: Knowing the result leaves the question of how the plant achieves it.
The chapter studies both the machinery and the energy-converting reactions.
items.example: Green plant photosynthetic structures and their associated reactions.
items.leads_to: Provides the roadmap from structures to reactions.
items.show: Zoom from the leaf into its working machinery.
needs_first: Photosynthesis uses light energy to synthesise organic compounds

key_question.q: Why study machinery as well as reactions?
key_question.a: A biological energy-conversion process requires both organised structures and the chemical events taking place within them; learning both links location with function.

items.content: 11.1 WHAT DO WE KNOW?
items.exam_note: Section heading.

items.content: Let us try to find out what we already know about photosynthesis. Some simple experiments you may have done in the earlier classes have shown that chlorophyll (green pigment of the leaf), light and CO₂ are required for photosynthesis to occur.
items.exam_note: This is a list of recalled requirements, not an exhaustive list of every raw material; do not infer that water is unnecessary.

terms.meaning: पत्ती का हरा pigment जो light पकड़ता है
terms.image: धूप में दिखती पत्ती का हरा हिस्सा

terms.meaning: रंग देने वाला पदार्थ जो कुछ light absorb करता है
terms.image: पत्ती को हरा दिखाने वाला पदार्थ

terms.meaning: carbon dioxide, एक carbon और दो oxygen atoms वाली gas
terms.image: हवा से पत्ती तक आती carbon dioxide

why: To explain food synthesis, identify what supplies energy and carbon.
Chlorophyll captures light energy, while CO₂ supplies carbon.
Earlier experiments establish chlorophyll, light and CO₂ as requirements.
items.example: The green pigment in a leaf exposed to light and carbon dioxide.
items.leads_to: The next experiment isolates green pigmentation and illumination as testable requirements.
items.show: Separate pigment, light input and carbon input.
items.level_extra: CO₂ is the carbon source; chlorophyll is not a food raw material. The CO₂ requirement is recalled here but not tested by the two leaf comparisons below.
needs_first: A pigment gives colour and can absorb light

key_question.q: How can an experiment show that a factor is necessary?
key_question.a: Compare otherwise similar conditions with the factor present and absent, and test for a photosynthetic outcome. Changing multiple factors together would obscure which one caused the difference.

items.content: You may have carried out the experiment to look for starch formation in two leaves – a variegated leaf or a leaf that was partially covered with black paper, and exposed to light. On testing these leaves for the presence of starch it was clear that photosynthesis occurred only in the green parts of the leaves in the presence of light.
items.exam_note: Match variegation with chlorophyll and black-paper covering with light. Starch is an indirect indicator; destarching avoids confusing old starch with newly formed starch.

terms.meaning: जिस पत्ती पर हरे और गैर-हरे हिस्से हों
terms.image: हरे और सफेद धब्बों वाली पत्ती

terms.meaning: food का जमा किया हुआ carbohydrate रूप
terms.image: आलू में जमा food

terms.meaning: light रोकने के लिए लगाया गया काला कागज़
terms.image: खिड़की पर पर्दा लगाकर रोशनी रोकना

why: To know whether greenness and light matter, compare regions that differ in one of these conditions.
Expose the variegated or partly covered leaf to light, then test it for starch.
Starch formation in green illuminated parts supports the requirements of chlorophyll and light.
items.example: Green versus non-green regions of one leaf; uncovered versus black-paper-covered regions of a green leaf.
items.leads_to: The experiment turns the introductory requirements into evidence-based conclusions while leaving CO₂ for a different test.
items.show: Mask, illuminate, test and map starch-positive regions.
items.level_extra: Build the two comparisons separately. Add the standard destarching and iodine-test explanation as outside support, not as steps printed on this page.
needs_first: Chlorophyll occurs in green leaf regions
Light is an energy source for photosynthesis
A controlled comparison changes one factor at a time

key_question.q: What standard precautions make the starch evidence meaningful?
key_question.a: Destarch the plant beforehand by keeping it in darkness long enough to use stored starch, then expose it under the experimental conditions. For the starch test, boil the leaf, remove chlorophyll using alcohol heated in a water bath, rinse and add iodine solution. Starch-containing regions become blue-black; alcohol must not be heated over a direct flame.

items.content: Another experiment you may have carried out where a part of a leaf is enclosed in a test tube containing some KOH soaked cotton (which absorbs CO₂), while the other half is exposed to air. The setup is then placed in light for some time. On testing for the presence of starch later in the two parts of the leaf, you must have found that the exposed part of the leaf tested positive for starch while the portion that was in the tube, tested negative. This showed that CO₂ was required for photosynthesis.
items.exam_note: Know the role of KOH, the positive and negative portions, and the inference that CO₂ is required; do not confuse CO₂ removal with oxygen removal.

terms.meaning: potassium hydroxide; यहाँ हवा से CO₂ हटाने वाला पदार्थ
terms.image: जैसे डिब्बे में रखा नमी सोखने वाला packet, पर यहाँ हटने वाली चीज़ CO₂ है

terms.meaning: carbon dioxide; एक carbon और दो oxygen atoms वाली gas
terms.image: साँस छोड़ते समय बाहर आने वाली हवा में मौजूद एक gas

terms.meaning: खाने में जमा रहने वाला carbohydrate
terms.image: आलू में जमा starch

terms.meaning: जाँच में जिस चीज़ को खोज रहे थे, वह मिली
terms.image: iodine डालने पर starch वाला हिस्सा नीला-काला दिखना

why: Need to test CO₂ rather than simply observe a leaf growing: remove CO₂ around one portion using KOH.
After light exposure, the air-exposed portion contains starch but the CO₂-deprived portion does not.
With other relevant conditions controlled, this supports CO₂ being necessary for photosynthetic starch formation.
items.example: Two portions of one leaf, one inside the test tube and one outside.
items.leads_to: The experiment moves from a visible starch-test result to an invisible requirement for a gas.
items.show: Enclose one leaf portion, remove CO₂, illuminate, and reveal contrasting iodine-test colours.
items.level_extra: NEET trap: KOH absorbs CO₂, not light or oxygen; light alone is insufficient for carbohydrate formation.
needs_first: Starch can be stored in a leaf
A controlled experiment changes one factor

key_question.q: Why use two portions of the same leaf?
key_question.a: It reduces differences due to leaf age, plant condition and initial reserves, making the comparison more informative than two unrelated leaves.

items.content: Can you explain how this conclusion could be drawn?
items.exam_note: Tests interpretation of an experiment, not merely recall of the reagent.
needs_first: Starch is evidence of photosynthetic carbohydrate formation

key_question.q: Why must the explanation mention controlled conditions?
key_question.a: A difference in starch formation identifies CO₂ as the relevant factor only if other necessary conditions are comparable and pre-existing starch has been removed.

items.content: 11.2 Early Experiments
It is interesting to learn about those simple experiments that led to a gradual development in our understanding of photosynthesis.
items.exam_note: Use as the organising link for scientist–contribution questions.
why: The process is not directly understood just by looking at a plant; simple experiments gradually developed the explanation.
Track the question each experiment answers rather than memorising disconnected names.
items.example: Priestley’s bell jars followed by Ingenhousz’s light–dark comparisons.
items.leads_to: Provides a running history of evidence for photosynthesis.
items.show: Add successive experimental findings to a timeline.
items.level_extra: Attach each scientist to the precise contribution demonstrated.

key_question.q: Why follow the experiments in sequence?
key_question.a: Each experiment answers a narrower question: whether plants restore air, whether light matters, and which plant parts release oxygen. Their sequence shows how evidence refines an explanation.

items.content: Joseph Priestley (1733-1804) in 1770 performed a series of experiments that revealed the essential role of air in the growth of green plants. Priestley, you may recall, discovered oxygen in 1774.
items.exam_note: Match Priestley with the bell-jar work and oxygen discovery; distinguish the two dates.

terms.meaning: हवा की वह gas जो साँस लेने और candle जलने में काम आती है
terms.image: ढकी candle का कुछ देर बाद बुझ जाना

why: Need to understand air’s role in plants: Priestley performed experiments in 1770.
The page separately records oxygen discovery in 1774, so observation and gas identification must remain distinct on the timeline.
items.example: A 1770 → 1774 timeline beside the bell-jar experiment.
items.leads_to: Sets up the evidence underlying the historical idea that plants restore air.
items.show: Place two distinct milestones on the timeline.
items.level_extra: NEET association: Priestley—not Ingenhousz—for the air-restoration hypothesis.
needs_first: An observation can precede identification of its cause

key_question.q: Why distinguish 1770 from 1774?
key_question.a: The page associates them with different achievements: experiments on plants and air versus discovery of oxygen. Combining them into one event loses that distinction.

items.content: Priestley observed that a candle burning in a closed space – a bell jar, soon gets extinguished (Figure 11.1 a, b, c, d). Similarly, a mouse would soon suffocate in a closed space. He concluded that a burning candle or an animal that breathe the air, both somehow, damage the air. But when he placed a mint plant in the same bell jar, he found that the mouse stayed alive and the candle continued to burn. Priestley hypothesised as follows: Plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove.
items.exam_note: Know the mint plant, candle, mouse and restoration-of-air conclusion. Priestley’s hypothesis is not the demonstration that sunlight is essential.

terms.meaning: घंटी जैसे आकार का glass ढक्कन, जो setup को बंद जगह में रखता है
terms.image: cake पर रखा बड़ा glass cover

terms.meaning: साँस के लिए ज़रूरी oxygen कम पड़ने से दम घुटना
terms.image: हवा का रास्ता बंद होने पर साँस लेने में परेशानी

terms.meaning: देखे हुए नतीजों को समझाने के लिए जाँचने लायक विचार दिया
terms.image: बुझी torch देखकर कहना कि शायद battery खत्म है, फिर जाँचना

terms.meaning: जो घट गया था उसे फिर से भरना
terms.image: खाली होती पानी की bottle को फिर भरना

why: Need to explain why a candle goes out and a mouse suffocates in closed air.
Adding a mint plant changes the reported outcome, leading Priestley to propose restoration of air.
Modern interpretation links oxygen consumption by breathing and burning with oxygen production by photosynthesis in light.
items.example: Mint plant, mouse and candle under a closed bell jar.
items.leads_to: Raises the next question: under which conditions can the plant restore air?
items.show: Deplete oxygen in one jar and replenish it through an illuminated plant in the comparison jar.
items.level_extra: Correct the misconception that plants only photosynthesise: they also respire. Avoid presenting the historical illustration as an indefinitely self-sustaining system.
needs_first: A closed jar does not freely exchange air

key_question.q: What does 'damage the air' mean in modern terms?
key_question.a: Combustion and aerobic respiration consume oxygen. In a closed jar its supply is finite, so it can become insufficient to sustain the flame or the animal.

items.content: Figure 11.1 shows four bell-jar panels. Upper row: (a) a mouse and a burning candle are enclosed without a plant; a rightward arrow leads to (b), showing an unlit candle and a collapsed mouse. Lower row: (c) a leafy potted plant, mouse and burning candle are enclosed together; a rightward arrow leads to (d), in which the plant remains, the mouse is upright and the candle is still burning. There is no vertical arrow connecting the two rows.
items.exam_note: Identify the experimental contrast and read the arrows correctly; do not infer an a→b→c→d sequence.
why: Need to compare what happens with and without a plant: the figure supplies two horizontal pairs.
Follow each arrow before comparing rows so initial conditions and outcomes are not confused.
items.example: Left-side Figure 11.1, upper and lower bell-jar pairs.
items.leads_to: Makes the evidence for air restoration visible.
items.show: Follow the two horizontal arrows and contrast the flames and mouse postures.
items.level_extra: The drawing does not itself test light versus darkness; that comparison belongs to Ingenhousz.
needs_first: Burning and respiration depend on the surrounding air

key_question.q: How should the figure be used to explain the experiment?
key_question.a: Read each horizontal pair as an initial state and its outcome, then compare the two outcomes. The plant is the conspicuous difference between the rows.

parts.content: (a): A closed bell jar containing a mouse and a burning candle, without a plant; the arrow points right to panel (b).
(b): The candle is extinguished and the mouse lies collapsed inside the bell jar without a plant; this is the outcome of (a).
(c): A leafy potted plant is enclosed with the mouse and burning candle; a rightward arrow leads to panel (d).
(d): The plant remains in the bell jar, the mouse is upright and the candle remains alight; this is the plant-present outcome following (c).

items.content: Figure 11.1 Priestley’s experiment

Can you imagine how Priestley would have conducted the experiment using a candle and a plant? Remember, he would need to rekindle the candle to test whether it burns after a few days. How many different ways can you think of to light the candle without disturbing the set-up?
items.exam_note: Experimental-design trap: opening the jar introduces an alternative explanation for renewed burning.
needs_first: Opening a jar allows air exchange
A fair comparison keeps other conditions similar

key_question.q: Why must the setup remain undisturbed?
key_question.a: Opening the jar admits fresh air and oxygen. Then a relit candle might burn because of the incoming air rather than because the plant restored the enclosed air.

items.content: Using a similar setup as the one used by Priestley, but by placing it once in the dark and once in the sunlight, Jan Ingenhousz (1730-1799) showed that sunlight is essential to the plant process that somehow purifies the air fouled by burning candles or breathing animals.
items.exam_note: Ingenhousz established the importance of sunlight; do not attribute the light–dark demonstration to Priestley.

terms.meaning: यहाँ हवा को फिर ऐसा बनाना कि candle जल सके और जानवर साँस ले सके
terms.image: कम हुई supply को फिर भर देना, धूल छानना नहीं

why: A plant restores air in Priestley’s account, but the needed conditions remain to be tested.
Ingenhousz compares darkness with sunlight and establishes the requirement of sunlight.
Interpret restoration as light-dependent photosynthetic oxygen release rather than a plant acting as a passive air filter.
items.example: A Priestley-like setup placed in darkness versus sunlight.
items.leads_to: Narrows the explanation from plant presence to plant activity in light.
items.show: Switch the illumination while holding the setup comparable.
items.level_extra: NEET trap: 'purification' here refers to the historical oxygen-restoration context, not removal of every air pollutant.
needs_first: Plants respire as well as photosynthesise

key_question.q: Why is the light–dark contrast important mechanistically?
key_question.a: Photosynthetic oxygen production depends on light-driven reactions, whereas plant respiration continues in darkness. A plant’s presence alone therefore does not guarantee net oxygen addition.

items.content: Ingenhousz in an elegant experiment with an aquatic plant showed that in bright sunlight, small bubbles were formed around the green parts while in the dark they did not. Later he identified these bubbles to be of oxygen. Hence he showed that it is only the green part of the plants that could release oxygen.
items.exam_note: Match Ingenhousz with oxygen bubbles, green parts and sunlight. The aquatic plant is not named on this page; do not invent a species.

terms.meaning: पानी में रहने या उगने वाला plant
terms.image: तालाब के पानी में डूबी हरी टहनियाँ

terms.meaning: plant के chlorophyll वाले हरे हिस्से
terms.image: हरी पत्ती और हरा नरम stem, भूरे तने से अलग

terms.meaning: पानी के अंदर gas के छोटे गोले
terms.image: पानी में straw से हवा छोड़ने पर ऊपर उठते गोले

why: Need visible evidence of what the plant releases: observe an aquatic plant in bright sunlight and darkness.
Bubbles form around green parts in sunlight, not in darkness; the gas is later identified as oxygen.
Green tissues contain the photosynthetic machinery that uses light and releases oxygen, explaining the observed restriction.
items.example: Around the green parts of the aquatic plant submerged in water.
items.leads_to: Completes the progression from restoration of air to light-dependent oxygen release by green plant parts.
items.show: Zoom to green tissues, form rising bubbles in light, then stop photosynthetic bubbling in darkness.
items.level_extra: NEET traps: bubbles are evidence of gas release, not automatic proof of gas identity; green parts include more than leaves; respiration does not stop in darkness.
needs_first: Gas released underwater may form bubbles
Photosynthesis and respiration are different processes

key_question.q: Why do the green parts produce oxygen in light?
key_question.a: Green parts contain chlorophyll-bearing chloroplasts that carry out photosynthesis. In its light reactions, water is split and oxygen is released.

items.content: It was not until about 1854 that Julius von Sachs provided evidence for production of glucose when plants grow. Glucose is usually stored as starch. His later studies showed that the green substance in plants (chlorophyll as we know it now) is located in special bodies (later called chloroplasts) within plant cells. He found that the green parts in plants is [are] where glucose is made, and that the glucose is usually stored as starch.
items.exam_note: Match Sachs with glucose production, starch storage and chlorophyll in chloroplasts; retain 'about 1854'.

terms.meaning: पौधे का हरा pigment, जो light पकड़ने में मदद करता है
terms.image: हरी पत्ती का रंग

terms.meaning: plant cell के अंदर chlorophyll रखने वाले छोटे हिस्से
terms.image: कमरे के अंदर सामान रखने की अलग अलमारी

terms.meaning: glucose की जुड़ी इकाइयों में रखा गया carbohydrate का भंडार
terms.image: आलू में जमा खाना

why: A growing plant needs a source of newly formed food; Sachs supplied evidence for glucose production.
His findings linked production with green parts and located the green pigment in chloroplasts.
The glucose produced is usually stored as starch, separating immediate sugar production from storage.
items.example: Zoom from a green leaf to its plant cells and then to chloroplasts containing chlorophyll.
items.leads_to: The next question is which components of light drive this food-producing activity most effectively.
items.show: zoom into the leaf and pack glucose units into starch
items.level_extra: NEET trap: chlorophyll is the pigment; chloroplast is its location. Do not invent an experimental procedure not described here.

key_question.q: Why is starch useful for storing carbohydrate rather than retaining large quantities as free glucose?
key_question.a: Starch is relatively insoluble and compact, so storing glucose units in it produces a smaller osmotic effect than storing the same units as separate soluble glucose molecules.

items.content: Now consider the interesting experiments done by T.W Engelmann (1843 – 1909). Using a prism he split light into its spectral components and then illuminated a green alga, Cladophora, placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. The bacteria were used to detect the sites of O₂ evolution. He observed that the bacteria accumulated mainly in the region of blue and red light of the split spectrum. A first action spectrum of photosynthesis was thus described. It resembles roughly the absorption spectra of chlorophyll a and b (discussed in section 11.4).
items.exam_note: Know Engelmann, Cladophora, aerobic bacteria, prism, blue/red regions and the first action spectrum. Bacteria detect oxygen; they are not the photosynthesising alga.

terms.meaning: light के अलग-अलग रंग या wavelength वाले हिस्से
terms.image: prism से निकली इंद्रधनुष जैसी पट्टी

terms.meaning: liquid में तैरते हुए छोटे कण या organisms
terms.image: पानी में तैरते छोटे कण

terms.meaning: respiration के लिए oxygen इस्तेमाल करने वाले bacteria
terms.image: जहाँ ज़रूरी चीज़ मिले वहाँ जुटती भीड़

terms.meaning: oxygen gas का बनकर बाहर निकलना
terms.image: पानी वाले पौधे से निकलते gas के बुलबुले

terms.meaning: किस wavelength पर photosynthesis कितना असरदार है, उसका नक्शा
terms.image: अलग काम करने वालों की performance chart

terms.meaning: pigment अलग-अलग wavelength की light कितनी पकड़ता है, उसका नक्शा
terms.image: अलग रंगों के लिए अलग ऊँचाई वाली bars

why: To compare colours, first separate light into spectral components with a prism.
Aerobic bacteria indicate where the illuminated Cladophora evolves oxygen.
Their blue/red accumulation links those spectral regions with greater photosynthetic activity.
items.example: Cladophora illuminated across the split spectrum while suspended aerobic bacteria collect near oxygen-producing regions.
items.leads_to: A biological response provides evidence for the wavelengths effective in photosynthesis, roughly matching chlorophyll absorption.
items.show: split light, illuminate the alga and cluster bacteria in blue and red
items.level_extra: Distinguish an activity measurement from pigment absorption. 'Mainly' does not mean photosynthesis is absent at every other wavelength.
needs_first: a prism separates light into colours

key_question.q: Why use aerobic bacteria rather than simply observing the alga?
key_question.a: Aerobic bacteria use oxygen in respiration and tend to accumulate where oxygen availability is greater. Their distribution acts as an indirect biological indicator of local oxygen production.

items.content: By the middle of the nineteenth century the key features of plant photosynthesis were known, namely, that plants could use light energy to make carbohydrates from CO₂ and water. The empirical equation representing the total process of photosynthesis for oxygen evolving organisms was then understood as:
items.exam_note: Keep the oxygen-evolving scope of this historical equation distinct from van Niel's broader formulation.

terms.meaning: देखे गए कुल inputs और outputs को छोटा करके लिखने वाली equation
terms.image: रसोई में सामग्री और तैयार खाने की छोटी सूची

why: Known observations needed a compact summary of what plants consume and produce.
By the mid-nineteenth century, light-driven carbohydrate formation from CO₂ and water was recognised.
items.example: Photosynthesis in oxygen-evolving green plants.
items.leads_to: The first equation is a historical overall summary, not a complete reaction mechanism.
items.show: collect observations into one input–output arrow
items.level_extra: Recall 'mid-nineteenth century' as context; prioritise the chemical meaning over memorising chronology alone.
needs_first: carbon dioxide and water are chemical substances

key_question.q: Why express this understanding as an empirical equation?
key_question.a: An empirical equation summarises the observed overall inputs and outputs without claiming to show the individual biochemical reactions.

items.content:
CO₂ + H₂O —Light→ [CH₂O] + O₂
where [CH₂O] represented a carbohydrate (e.g., glucose, a six-carbon sugar).
items.exam_note: Trap: [CH₂O] represents carbohydrate composition, not the molecular formula of glucose.

terms.meaning: carbohydrate की composition दिखाने वाला छोटा संकेत, पूरा glucose molecule नहीं
terms.image: पूरी दीवार के बजाय उसकी एक दोहराई जाने वाली ईंट

why: A general equation needs a compact way to represent carbohydrate.
The book uses [CH₂O], with six-carbon glucose as an example.
Distinguishing a composition unit from a whole molecule prevents incorrect formula recall.
items.example: Glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆, corresponding to six CH₂O composition units.
items.leads_to: This short equation does not establish which reactant supplies evolved oxygen.
items.show: expand one carbohydrate composition unit into a six-carbon formula
items.level_extra: Read symbols and subscripts carefully; do not infer oxygen's source merely from a balanced equation.
needs_first: reactants and products in chemical equations

key_question.q: Why must [CH₂O] not be read as the molecular formula of glucose?
key_question.a: It expresses a carbohydrate composition unit. Glucose has the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆, so its six carbons are not represented by interpreting CH₂O as a complete glucose molecule.

items.content: A milestone contribution to the understanding of photosynthesis was that made by a microbiologist, Cornelius van Niel (1897-1985), who, based on his studies of purple and green bacteria, demonstrated that photosynthesis is essentially a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from a suitable oxidisable compound reduces carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. This can be expressed by:
items.exam_note: Match van Niel with purple/green bacterial studies and the general hydrogen-donor concept.

terms.meaning: ऐसा compound जो electrons देकर खुद oxidised हो सके
terms.image: एक व्यक्ति सामान देता है ताकि दूसरा उसे ले सके

terms.meaning: electrons मिलने से chemical हालत बदलती है; यहाँ CO₂ से carbohydrate बनने में मदद मिलती है
terms.image: एक तरफ से निकले सामान का दूसरी तरफ पहुँचना

terms.meaning: जिसके चलने के लिए light की ज़रूरत हो

items.content: 11.4 How many Types of Pigments are Involved in Photosynthesis?

Looking at plants have you ever wondered why and how there are so many shades of green in their leaves – even in the same plant? We can look for an answer to this question by trying to separate the leaf pigments of any green plant through paper chromatography. A chromatographic separation of the leaf pigments shows that the colour that we see in leaves is not due to a single pigment but due to four

items.content: These graphs, together, show that most of the photosynthesis takes place in the blue and red regions of the spectrum; some photosynthesis does take place at the other wavelengths of the visible spectrum. Let us see how this happens. Though chlorophyll is the major pigment responsible for trapping light, other thylakoid pigments like chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids, which are called accessory pigments, also absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a. Indeed, they not only enable a wider range of wavelength of incoming light to be utilised for photosynthesis but also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

items.content: When only PS I is functional, the electron is circulated within the photosystem and the phosphorylation occurs due to cyclic flow of electrons (Figure 11.6). A possible location where this could be happening is in the stroma lamellae. While the membrane or lamellae of the grana have both PS I and PS II the stroma lamellae membranes lack PS II as well as NADP reductase enzyme. The excited electron does not pass on to NADP⁺ but is cycled back to the PS I complex through the electron transport chain (Figure 11.6). The cyclic flow hence, results only in the synthesis of ATP, but not of NADPH + H⁺. Cyclic photophosphorylation also occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm are available for excitation.

items.content: Let us now try and understand how actually ATP is synthesised in the chloroplast. The chemiosmotic hypothesis has been put forward to explain the mechanism. Like in respiration, in photosynthesis too, ATP synthesis is linked to development of a proton gradient across a membrane. This time these are the membranes of thylakoid. There is one difference though, here the proton accumulation is towards the inside of the membrane, i.e., in the lumen. In respiration, protons accumulate in the intermembrane space of the mitochondria when electrons move through the ETS (Chapter 12).
items.exam_note: Chloroplast accumulation: lumen, not stroma. Mitochondrial accumulation: intermembrane space, not matrix.

items.content: 11.7 WHERE ARE THE ATP AND NADPH USED?

We learnt that the products of light reaction are ATP, NADPH and O₂. Of these O₂ diffuses out of the chloroplast while ATP and NADPH are used to drive the processes leading to the synthesis of food, more accurately, sugars.

items.content: This is the biosynthetic phase of photosynthesis. This process does not directly depend on the presence of light but is dependent on the products of the light reaction, i.e., ATP and NADPH, besides CO₂ and H₂O. You may wonder how this could be verified; it is simple: immediately after light becomes unavailable, the biosynthetic process continues for some time, and then stops. If then, light is made available, the synthesis starts again.

The use of radioactive ¹⁴C by him in algal photosynthesis studies led to the discovery that the first CO₂ fixation product was a 3-carbon organic acid. He also contributed to working out the complete biosynthetic pathway; hence it was called Calvin cycle after him. The first product identified was 3-phosphoglyceric acid or in short PGA.

items.content: Scientists also tried to know whether all plants have PGA as the first product of CO₂ fixation, or whether any other product was formed in other plants. Experiments conducted over a wide range of plants led to the discovery of another group of plants, where the first stable product of CO₂ fixation was again an organic acid, but one which had 4 carbon atoms in it. This acid was identified to be oxaloacetic acid or OAA. Since then CO₂ assimilation during photosynthesis was said to be of two main types: those plants in which the first product of CO₂ fixation is a C₃ acid (PGA), i.e., the C₃ pathway, and those in which the first product was a C₄ acid (OAA), i.e., the C₄ pathway. These two groups of plants showed other associated characteristics that we will discuss later.
items.exam_note: Match C₃ with PGA and C₄ with OAA; the naming criterion is the first stable fixation product.

items.content: 11.7.1 The Primary Acceptor of CO₂

Let us now ask ourselves a question that was asked by the scientists who were struggling to understand the ‘dark reaction’. How many carbon atoms would a molecule have which after accepting (fixing) CO₂, would have 3 carbons (of PGA)?

key_question.q: Why is subtracting one carbon from one PGA molecule misleading?
key_question.a: It assumes fixation produces just one three-carbon molecule. In the Calvin-cycle reaction, a five-carbon acceptor combines with one-carbon CO₂ and yields two three-carbon PGA molecules: 5 + 1 = 2 × 3.

items.content: Did any of you think of this possibility? Do not worry; the scientists also took a long time and conducted many experiments to reach this conclusion. items.content: 11.7.2 The Calvin Cycle
Calvin and his co-workers then worked out the whole pathway and showed that the pathway operated in a cyclic manner; the RuBP was regenerated.

key_question.a: RuBP is regenerated during the pathway. Thus the acceptor used in fixation is formed again rather than simply being exhausted at the end of a one-way sequence.

items.content: Let us now see how the Calvin pathway operates and where the sugar is synthesised. Let us at the outset understand very clearly that the Calvin pathway occurs in all photosynthetic plants; it does not matter whether they have C₃ or C₄ (or any other) pathways (Figure 11.8).

key_question.a: In C₄ plants, initial fixation into a four-carbon compound precedes delivery of CO₂ to the Calvin cycle. The initial fixation route and the subsequent Calvin cycle are different parts of carbon assimilation, not mutually exclusive alternatives.

items.content: For ease of understanding, the Calvin cycle can be described under three stages: carboxylation, reduction and regeneration.
items.exam_note: Know the three stages and their order; this page develops only carboxylation.

key_question.q: Why is this three-stage map useful?
key_question.a: It separates three different jobs: bringing carbon into the pathway, converting the fixed carbon toward carbohydrate, and restoring the acceptor. Students can then attach individual reactions to their job instead of memorising an unstructured list.

items.content: 1. Carboxylation – Carboxylation is the fixation of CO₂ into a stable organic intermediate. Carboxylation is the most crucial step of the Calvin cycle where CO₂ is utilised for the carboxylation of RuBP. This reaction is catalysed by the enzyme RuBP carboxylase which results in the formation of two molecules of 3-PGA. Since this enzyme also has an oxygenation activity it would be more correct to call it RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase or RuBisCO.
items.exam_note: Know RuBisCO's full name, dual activity, substrate RuBP and yield of two 3-PGA molecules per RuBP carboxylation. OAA is not this reaction's product.

The Calvin cycle has three stages

key_question.q: How is the two-PGA yield consistent with the carbon numbers?
key_question.a: Five-carbon RuBP receives the one carbon of CO₂. The resulting unstable six-carbon intermediate splits into two three-carbon 3-PGA molecules. Thus the first stable product can be C₃ even though six carbons pass through the immediate intermediate.

items.content: Calvin cycle: atmospheric CO₂ + H₂O enters stage 1, Carboxylation, with ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. The clockwise path proceeds to 3-phosphoglycerate, then stage 2, Reduction, then triose phosphate. ATP + NADPH enter reduction; ADP + Pᵢ + NADP⁺ leave it. A downward branch from triose phosphate leads to sucrose, starch. The continuing cycle passes through stage 3, Regeneration, where ATP enters and ADP leaves, and returns to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate.
items.exam_note: Identify stages, carbon compounds and energy-input arrows; ATP is used in two stages, NADPH in reduction.

Reduction forms carbohydrate using ATP and NADPH.
Regeneration renews the acceptor so the cycle continues.

key_question.q: How do the arrows distinguish carbon flow from energy support?
key_question.a: The main loop joins carbon compounds, whereas side arrows bring ATP and NADPH into reduction and ATP into regeneration, with spent carriers leaving.

parts.content: Atmosphere — arrow points toward the CO₂ input.
CO₂ + H₂O — inputs shown entering carboxylation.
Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate — regenerated compound entering carboxylation.
1 Carboxylation — first stage, between RuBP plus CO₂ input and 3-phosphoglycerate.
ADP — leaves the regeneration stage.
3 Regeneration — returning route from triose phosphate to RuBP.
3-phosphoglycerate — compound following carboxylation and entering reduction.
ATP — enters regeneration.
ATP + NADPH — enter reduction.
2 Reduction — stage leading from 3-phosphoglycerate to triose phosphate. The adjacent + belongs to the ATP + NADPH input.
Triose phosphate — receives the reduction arrow; branches toward sucrose, starch and toward regeneration.
ADP + Pᵢ + NADP⁺ — products leaving after use of ATP and NADPH during reduction.
Sucrose, starch — carbohydrate products reached by the downward branch from triose phosphate.

items.content: Figure 11.8 The Calvin cycle proceeds in three stages : (1) carboxylation, during which CO₂ combines with ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate; (2) reduction, during which carbohydrate is formed at the expense of the photochemically made ATP and NADPH; and (3) regeneration during which the CO₂ acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate is formed again so that the cycle continues

The fixation of six molecules of CO₂ and 6 turns of the cycle are required for the formation of one molecule of glucose from the pathway.

key_question.q: Why does suppressing photorespiration help productivity?
key_question.a: Rubisco's oxygenase activity leads to photorespiration, which consumes resources and releases previously fixed carbon without net sugar production. Concentrating CO₂ near Rubisco strongly suppresses this loss and favours carboxylation.

items.content: Two connected cells show the Hatch and Slack pathway. The upper mesophyll cell receives atmospheric CO₂, shown as HCO₃⁻ joining phosphoenol-pyruvate at Fixation. A downward arrow leads to C₄ acid, then Transport through the connection labelled Plasmodesmata into the lower bundle sheath cell. Its C₄ acid undergoes Decarboxylation. One branch releases CO₂ upward to Fixation by Calvin cycle; the other produces C₃ acid, which moves upward through Transport back to the mesophyll cell. There C₃ acid passes through Regeneration to phosphoenol-pyruvate. Plasma membrane and Cell wall are identified at the upper cell boundary.

parts.content: Atmospheric CO₂ — source arrow enters the mesophyll cell and leads to HCO₃⁻.
Mesophyll cell — identifies the upper green cell containing Fixation and Regeneration.
Plasma membrane — pointer identifies the inner boundary of the mesophyll cell.
Cell wall — pointer identifies the outer boundary around the mesophyll cell.
HCO₃⁻ — bicarbonate input beneath atmospheric CO₂, joined with phosphoenol-pyruvate by the line leading to Fixation.
Phosphoenol-pyruvate — participates in Fixation and receives the curved arrow from Regeneration.
Fixation — box receiving the PEP and HCO₃⁻ inputs and pointing downward to C₄ acid.
C₄ acid — product below Fixation, moving toward the upper Transport box.
Transport — upper box on the downward C₄-acid route from mesophyll to bundle sheath cell.
Plasmo-desmata [Plasmodesmata] — printed over two lines; pointer identifies the channels connecting the two cells.
Bundle sheath cell — identifies the lower cell containing C₄-acid decarboxylation and fixation by Calvin cycle.
C₄ acid — incoming acid in the bundle sheath cell, with a downward arrow to Decarboxylation.
Decarboxylation — C₄ acid enters this box; outgoing branches lead to CO₂ and C₃ acid.
CO₂ — released carbon dioxide, with an upward arrow to Fixation by Calvin cycle.
Fixation by Calvin cycle — label above the arrow receiving released CO₂.
C₃ acid — 3-carbon product beside Decarboxylation, with an upward arrow toward Transport.
Transport — lower box on the upward C₃-acid return route from bundle sheath to mesophyll.
C₃ acid — returned 3-carbon acid in mesophyll, with an upward arrow to Regeneration.
Regeneration — receives the upward C₃-acid arrow and sends a curved arrow to phosphoenol-pyruvate.

items.content: 11.9 PHOTORESPIRATION

Let us try and understand one more process that creates an important difference between C₃ and C₄ plants – Photorespiration. To understand photorespiration we have to know a little bit more about the first step of the Calvin pathway – the first CO₂ fixation step. This is the reaction where RuBP combines with CO₂ to form 2 molecules of 3PGA, that is catalysed by RuBisCO.
items.exam_note: Recall substrate, enzyme and two 3PGA products before learning oxygenation.

items.content: In the photorespiratory pathway, there is neither synthesis of sugars, nor of ATP. Rather it results in the release of CO₂ with the utilisation of ATP. In the photorespiratory pathway there is no synthesis of ATP or NADPH. The biological function of photorespiration is not known yet.

items.content: In C₄ plants photorespiration does not occur. This is because they have a mechanism that increases the concentration of CO₂ at the enzyme site. This takes place when the C₄ acid from the mesophyll is broken down in the bundle sheath cells to release CO₂ – this results in increasing the intracellular concentration of CO₂. In turn, this ensures that the RuBisCO functions as a carboxylase minimising the oxygenase activity.
items.exam_note: Key chain: C₄ acid → bundle sheath breakdown → high CO₂ → carboxylase favoured. C₄ plants do have RuBisCO.

items.content: 11.10 Factors affecting Photosynthesis

An understanding of the factors that affect photosynthesis is necessary. The rate of photosynthesis is very important in determining the yield of plants including crop plants. Photosynthesis is under the influence of several factors, both internal (plant) and external. The plant factors include the number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ concentration and the amount of chlorophyll. The plant or internal factors are dependent on the genetic predisposition and the growth of the plant.
items.exam_note: Recognise internal factors in list-based questions; internal CO₂ concentration is specifically included.

key_question.q: How can leaf orientation, mesophyll and chloroplasts influence photosynthesis?
key_question.a: Leaf orientation affects interception of light. Mesophyll is the internal leaf tissue containing photosynthetic cells, and chloroplasts are the sites of photosynthesis. Their development and abundance influence the plant’s capacity to use light and fix carbon.

items.content: The external factors would include the availability of sunlight, temperature, CO₂ concentration and water. As a plant photosynthesises, all these factors will simultaneously affect its rate. Hence, though several factors interact and simultaneously affect photosynthesis or CO₂ fixation, usually one factor is the major cause or is the one that limits the rate. Hence, at any point the rate will be determined by the factor available at sub-optimal levels.
items.exam_note: Trap: simultaneous influence does not mean every factor is equally rate-limiting.

items.content: When several factors affect any [bio] chemical process, Blackman’s (1905) Law of Limiting Factors comes into effect. This states the following: If a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, then its rate will be determined by the factor which is nearest to its minimal value: it is the factor which directly affects the process if its quantity is changed.
items.exam_note: Learn Blackman, 1905, the law’s wording and its experimental application.

key_question.a: Photosynthesis includes enzyme-mediated biochemical reactions. Very low temperature can slow these reactions, so light capture alone cannot ensure rapid carbon fixation.

items.content: 11.10.2 Carbon dioxide Concentration

Carbon dioxide is the major limiting factor for photosynthesis. The concentration of CO₂ is very low in the atmosphere (between 0.03 and 0.04 per cent). Increase in concentration upto 0.05 per cent can cause an increase in CO₂ fixation rates; beyond this the levels can become damaging over longer periods.
items.exam_note: Learn 0.03–0.04%, upto 0.05%, and the qualification that higher levels can damage over longer periods.

items.content: The C₃ and C₄ plants respond differently to CO₂ concentrations. At low light conditions neither group responds to high CO₂ conditions. At high light intensities, both C₃ and C₄ plants show increase in the rates of photosynthesis. What is important to note is that the C₄ plants show saturation at about 360 µlL⁻¹ while C₃ responds to increased CO₂ concentration and saturation is seen only beyond 450 µlL⁻¹. Thus, current availability of CO₂ levels is limiting to the C₃ plants.
items.exam_note: Remember low-light non-response, high-light response, C₄ ≈360 µlL⁻¹ and C₃ >450 µlL⁻¹. Saturation is not cessation of photosynthesis.
