terms.image: एक बड़े डिब्बे में छोटे हिस्से का माप

terms.meaning: carbon fixation के अलग रास्तों वाले plants, जिनके पहले stable products में 3 या 4 carbon होते हैं
terms.image: एक मंज़िल तक जाने वाले दो अलग रास्ते

why: Ask whether extra CO₂ helps when light itself is scarce.
Neither group responds under low light; both respond under high light.
C₄ saturates near 360 µlL⁻¹ while C₃ continues responding beyond that, saturating only beyond 450 µlL⁻¹.
items.example: Compare C₃ and C₄ leaves under the same light conditions while changing CO₂.
items.leads_to: CO₂ limitation depends on both the plant pathway and the availability of light.
items.show: Hold light fixed, raise CO₂ and flatten the C₄ response before the C₃ response.
items.level_extra: Build the response comparison in two stages: low light first, high light next. Do not confuse a plateau with zero photosynthesis.
needs_first: light reactions supply energy for carbon fixation

key_question.q: Why does adding CO₂ fail to increase photosynthesis in low light?
key_question.a: When light restricts energy supply, extra carbon substrate cannot remove that restriction. The limiting factor must be relieved before enrichment can produce its expected response.

items.content: The fact that C₃ plants respond to higher CO₂ concentration by showing increased rates of photosynthesis leading to higher productivity has been used for some greenhouse crops such as tomatoes and bell pepper. They are allowed to grow in carbon dioxide enriched atmosphere that leads to higher yields.
items.exam_note: Book examples: tomatoes and bell pepper; link CO₂ enrichment to C₃ productivity.

terms.meaning: ऐसी हवा जिसमें CO₂ की मात्रा बढ़ाई गई हो
terms.image: greenhouse के अंदर हवा की बनावट को नियंत्रित करना

terms.meaning: फसल से मिलने वाली उपयोगी पैदावार
terms.image: कटाई पर इकट्ठे हुए टमाटरों की टोकरियाँ

why: The grower wants more useful crop production.
C₃ crops respond to higher CO₂ with increased photosynthesis.
Tomatoes and bell pepper grown in enriched greenhouse air give higher yields.
items.example: Tomatoes and bell pepper in greenhouses.
items.leads_to: A limiting-factor principle becomes a cultivation technique.
items.show: Enrich greenhouse air, increase carbon assimilation and fill more harvest baskets.
items.level_extra: Recall both named crops and avoid claiming unlimited benefit from enrichment.
needs_first: photosynthesis supplies organic material for growth

key_question.q: Why can enrichment increase yield, and what limits this application?
key_question.a: More available CO₂ can support greater carbon assimilation and biomass formation. The benefit depends on other requirements, such as adequate light, water and suitable temperature, not becoming limiting.

items.content: 11.10.3 Temperature
The dark reactions being enzymatic are temperature controlled. Though the light reactions are also temperature sensitive they are affected to a much lesser extent.
items.exam_note: Dark reactions are more temperature sensitive; light reactions are not completely temperature independent.

terms.meaning: enzyme की मदद से होने वाला काम
terms.image: काम की रफ्तार बढ़ाने वाला मददगार

terms.meaning: carbon fixation की reactions जो सीधे light इस्तेमाल नहीं करतीं
terms.image: पहले जमा की गई energy से आगे चलता काम

why: Carbon fixation needs enzymes to carry out its reactions.
Enzyme activity changes with temperature.
Dark reactions are temperature controlled; light reactions are affected less.
items.example: Carbon-fixation reactions in the chloroplast stroma, contrasted with light reactions at thylakoid membranes.
items.leads_to: Changing temperature can alter carbon assimilation even if light remains unchanged.
items.show: Change a thermometer and vary enzyme reaction speed.
items.level_extra: Trap: less temperature sensitive does not mean insensitive; dark does not mean night-only.

key_question.q: How does temperature affect enzyme-controlled reactions?
key_question.a: Warming within a suitable range can increase enzyme-catalysed reaction rates. Excessive heat can impair enzyme structure and activity, so the response is not an unlimited increase.

items.content: The C₄ plants respond to higher temperatures and show higher rate of photosynthesis while C₃ plants have a much lower temperature optimum.
items.exam_note: C₄ has a higher temperature optimum than C₃; the page provides no exact optimum temperatures.

terms.meaning: वह temperature जिस पर photosynthesis सबसे अच्छा चलता है
terms.image: काम करने के लिए सबसे आरामदेह गर्मी, न बहुत ठंड न बहुत गरम

why: Different pathways need not perform best at the same temperature.
C₄ plants perform favourably at higher temperatures; C₃ plants have a lower optimum.
CO₂ concentration in C₄ plants helps reduce photorespiratory loss at higher temperatures.
items.example: Compare the photosynthetic temperature responses of C₃ and C₄ leaves.
items.leads_to: The photosynthetic pathway helps determine environmental performance.
items.show: Place the C₄ temperature-response peak to the warmer side of the C₃ peak.
items.level_extra: Do not invent numerical temperature optima or assume C₄ photosynthesis rises indefinitely with heat.

key_question.q: Why can the C₄ pathway favour photosynthesis at higher temperatures?
key_question.a: At higher temperatures photorespiration can increasingly reduce net carbon gain in C₃ plants. The CO₂-concentrating mechanism of C₄ plants suppresses this loss and contributes to their advantage.

items.content: The temperature optimum for photosynthesis of different plants also depends on the habitat that they are adapted to. Tropical plants have a higher temperature optimum than the plants adapted to temperate climates.
items.exam_note: Habitat adaptation also matters; do not explain every temperature difference solely through C₃ or C₄.

terms.meaning: वह जगह और हालात जहाँ plant रहता है
terms.image: घर के साथ आसपास का मौसम

terms.meaning: धरती के गर्म tropical इलाकों से जुड़ा
terms.image: साल के बड़े हिस्से में गर्म रहने वाला इलाका

terms.meaning: tropical इलाकों से आम तौर पर ठंडे, मौसम बदलने वाले इलाकों का climate
terms.image: जहाँ गर्मी और सर्दी का फर्क साफ दिखता है

why: Plants from different habitats experience different temperature conditions.
Photosynthetic temperature optima depend on habitat adaptation.
Tropical plants have higher optima than temperate-adapted plants.
items.example: Tropical habitats compared with temperate climates; no particular species are named here.
items.leads_to: There is no single photosynthetic optimum applicable to all plants.
items.show: Compare warmer and cooler habitat backgrounds and shift the optimum marker.
items.level_extra: Keep habitat adaptation distinct from the C₃–C₄ classification.

key_question.q: Why should habitat adaptation influence the optimum?
key_question.a: Plants adapted to different thermal environments have physiological machinery suited to those environments. Consequently, one temperature need not give the best photosynthetic performance in plants from different climates.

items.content: 11.10.4 Water

Even though water is one of the reactants in the light reaction, the effect of water as a factor is more through its effect on the plant, rather than directly on photosynthesis. Water stress causes the stomata to close hence reducing the CO₂ availability. Besides, water stress also makes leaves wilt, thus, reducing the surface area of the leaves and their metabolic activity as well.
items.exam_note: Main effect is indirect. Learn both branches: stomatal closure → less CO₂, and wilting → reduced surface area and metabolic activity.

terms.meaning: plant की ज़रूरत के मुकाबले पानी कम पड़ना
terms.image: पानी न मिलने पर गमले का plant झुकना

terms.meaning: पत्ती के छोटे pores जिनसे gases आती-जाती हैं
terms.image: हवा आने-जाने की छोटी खिड़कियाँ

terms.meaning: पानी कम होने से पत्ती का ढीला पड़कर झुकना
terms.image: धूप में पानी बिना रखा मुरझाया पौधा

terms.meaning: plant के अंदर चलने वाली chemical reactions का काम
terms.image: घर के अंदर साथ-साथ चल रहे कई काम

why: A water-stressed plant must limit further water loss.
Stomata close, reducing CO₂ availability.
Water stress also causes wilting, reducing leaf surface area and metabolic activity.
items.example: A water-stressed potted plant: zoom from drooping leaves to their stomatal pores.
items.leads_to: Water shortage can impose a carbon-supply limitation as well as impair leaf functioning.
items.show: Split water stress into two branches: close stomata and droop the leaf.
items.level_extra: Correct the misconception that water limits photosynthesis chiefly by directly running out as a substrate; retain the book's emphasis on indirect effects.
needs_first: water as a reactant in light reactions

key_question.q: Why does stomatal closure conserve water but restrict photosynthesis?
key_question.a: Stomatal pores provide a route both for water vapour to escape and for CO₂ to diffuse into the leaf. Closing them reduces water loss but also restricts carbon entry.

items.content: SUMMARY
items.exam_note: Chapter recap heading.

items.content: Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis. During this process carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is taken in by leaves through stomata and used for making carbohydrates, principally glucose and starch.
items.exam_note: Distinguish the carbon source from the energy source; stomata are the gas-entry route.

terms.meaning: रोशनी की मदद से अपना organic food बनाने की प्रक्रिया
terms.image: धूप में लगी पत्ती food बनाने की छोटी factory जैसी

terms.meaning: पत्ती की सतह के छोटे pores जिनसे gases आती-जाती हैं
terms.image: कमरे में हवा आने की छोटी खिड़कियाँ

terms.meaning: glucose और starch जैसे carbon वाले food compounds
terms.image: चीनी में sugar और आलू में जमा starch

why: A plant needs both carbon material and energy to make organic food.
Atmospheric CO₂ enters leaves through stomata.
Photosynthesis uses this carbon to produce carbohydrates.
items.example: Atmosphere → leaf stomata → photosynthetic cells.
items.leads_to: Carbon entry must be linked to the chloroplast reactions that incorporate it.
items.show: Trace CO₂ entering a pore and its carbon joining carbohydrate.
items.level_extra: Glucose is a sugar; starch is a storage carbohydrate. Do not treat sunlight as a material source of carbon.

key_question.q: Why must a plant take in carbon dioxide even when it receives sunlight?
key_question.a: Light supplies energy, not carbon atoms. CO₂ supplies carbon that can be incorporated into organic compounds.

items.content: Photosynthesis takes place only in the green parts of the plants, mainly the leaves. Within the leaves, the mesophyll cells have a large number of chloroplasts that are responsible for CO₂ fixation. Within the chloroplasts, the membranes are sites for the light reaction, while the chemosynthetic pathway [biosynthetic carbon-fixing pathway] occurs in the stroma.
items.exam_note: NEET location trap: light reactions at thylakoid membranes, Calvin cycle in stroma, not the reverse.

terms.meaning: पत्ती के अंदर का photosynthesis करने वाला tissue
terms.image: पत्ती की दो बाहरी परतों के बीच का हरा हिस्सा

terms.meaning: हरे cell के अंदर photosynthesis के काम करने वाले छोटे organelles
terms.image: एक factory के अंदर छोटी काम करने वाली units

terms.meaning: chloroplast के अंदर membranes के बाहर का fluid वाला हिस्सा
terms.image: कमरे में रखी shelves के चारों ओर की जगह

why: Photosynthesis needs organised sites for different jobs.
Mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts.
Membranes and stroma provide different locations for light reactions and carbon fixation.
items.example: Green leaf → mesophyll cell → chloroplast → thylakoid membrane or stroma.
items.leads_to: Products made at membranes must become available to carbon-fixing reactions in the stroma.
items.show: Zoom inward and colour-code membrane and stroma.
items.level_extra: Green stems can also photosynthesise; the page says mainly leaves, not leaves alone.

key_question.q: Why is the membrane location important for light reactions?
key_question.a: Thylakoid membranes organise photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase, and separate two regions so that a proton gradient can form.

items.content: Photosynthesis has two stages: the light reaction and the carbon fixing reactions.
items.exam_note: Do not infer that 'light-independent' means the Calvin cycle runs only at night.

terms.meaning: CO₂ के carbon को organic compounds में जोड़ने वाले reactions
terms.image: खुले सामान को किसी तैयार ढाँचे में जोड़ना

why: Making carbohydrate needs usable energy and incorporation of carbon.
The light reaction supplies ATP and NADPH.
Carbon-fixing reactions use these supplies.
items.example: Two linked reaction sets inside one chloroplast.
items.leads_to: The next concepts explain energy capture first and its use in carbon fixation later.
items.show: Connect two labelled stages with ATP and NADPH arrows.
items.level_extra: Separate direct use of photons from dependence on products of light reactions.

key_question.q: Why should they be taught as connected rather than independent processes?
key_question.a: The carbon fixation cycle utilises ATP and NADPH synthesised in the light reaction, so the products of one stage support the other.

items.content: In the light reaction the light energy is absorbed by the pigments present in the antenna, and funnelled to special chlorophyll a molecules called reaction centre chlorophylls.
items.exam_note: Distinguish light-harvesting antenna pigments from reaction-centre chlorophyll a.

terms.meaning: कई pigments का light पकड़कर energy पहुँचाने वाला समूह
terms.image: कई लोग अलग-अलग जगह से सामान एक counter तक पहुँचाएँ

terms.meaning: खास chlorophyll a molecules जहाँ light energy electron transfer शुरू कराती है
terms.image: कई रास्तों से आया सामान एक मुख्य dispatch counter पर पहुँचे

why: A reaction centre needs a supply of captured light energy.
Antenna pigments absorb light and funnel energy to it.
Excitation at the reaction centre supports electron transfer.
items.example: A photosystem embedded in a thylakoid membrane.
items.leads_to: Energy harvesting prepares the reaction centre for the electron-transfer sequence.
items.show: Converge excitation flashes from antenna pigments onto chlorophyll a.
items.level_extra: Show energy moving through the antenna, not the same electron hopping through all antenna pigments.

key_question.q: Why collect light with an antenna rather than rely on a reaction centre alone?
key_question.a: A collection of pigment molecules increases the opportunity to capture light and transfer excitation energy to the reaction centre, where charge separation can begin.

items.content: There are two photosystems, PS I and PS II. PS I has a 700 nm absorbing chlorophyll a P700 molecule at its reaction centre, while PS II has a P680 reaction centre that absorbs red light at 680 nm.
items.exam_note: High-yield pairing: PS I–P700–700 nm; PS II–P680–680 nm. Numerical names do not give electron-flow order.

terms.meaning: light पकड़ने और electron transfer शुरू करने वाली pigment-protein units
terms.image: एक ही factory की दो अलग light-powered workstations

terms.meaning: wavelength नापने की बहुत छोटी length unit, nanometre
terms.image: ruler की unit से भी बेहद छोटी दूरी की unit

why: The two reaction centres must be distinguished without confusing their roles.
PS I is associated with P700 and PS II with P680.
Their numerals must not be mistaken for the order of electron flow.
items.example: PS I and PS II in the chloroplast thylakoid membrane.
items.leads_to: The next sequence must be read as PS II → PS I.
items.show: Pair each photosystem with its reaction-centre label and wavelength.
items.level_extra: The wavelengths refer to characteristic reaction-centre absorption, not to the only light absorbed by the entire antenna.

key_question.q: Why does PS II come before PS I in the electron-transfer sequence despite the numerals?
key_question.a: The numbering reflects their order of discovery, not the order of non-cyclic electron flow.

items.content: After absorbing light, electrons are excited and transferred through PS II and PS I and finally to NAD [NADP⁺] forming NADH [NADPH].
items.exam_note: Correct the printed biochemical error: NADP⁺ → NADPH; non-cyclic sequence starts with PS II.

terms.meaning: energy मिलने पर electron का ऊँची energy वाली हालत में जाना
terms.image: गेंद को नीचे से ऊँची shelf तक उठाना

terms.meaning: electrons लेकर carbon fixation को reducing power देने वाला carrier
terms.image: charge लेकर अगले काम तक पहुँचने वाली rechargeable battery

why: Carbon fixation requires a supply of reducing power.
Light excites electrons that pass through PS II and PS I.
Their transfer to NADP⁺ produces NADPH for biosynthesis.
items.example: Thylakoid electron transport, ending with NADPH formation on the stromal side.
items.leads_to: NADPH links light capture to the reduction steps of the Calvin cycle.
items.show: Trace electrons from PS II through PS I to NADP⁺.
items.level_extra: Name the NADH/NADPH trap explicitly; use the correct carrier in all teaching answers.
needs_first: PS II and PS I identities

key_question.q: Why must the printed NAD/NADH wording be corrected?
key_question.a: The reducing product of the standard photosynthetic light reaction is NADPH, formed from NADP⁺, not NADH from NAD. The page later correctly identifies NADPH as a product used in carbon fixation.

items.content: During this process a proton gradient is created across the membrane of the thylakoid. The breakdown of the protons [proton] gradient due to movement through the F₀ part of the ATPase enzyme releases enough energy for synthesis of ATP.
items.exam_note: Chemiosmosis: lumen-to-stroma proton return, F₀ proton channel and F₁ catalysis. ATP is not formed simply because electrons touch ADP.

terms.meaning: membrane के दो तरफ H⁺ की मात्रा और electrical condition में फर्क
terms.image: बाँध के दोनों तरफ पानी के level में फर्क

terms.meaning: ATP synthase का membrane में लगा H⁺ जाने का रास्ता
terms.image: बाँध में turbine तक पानी ले जाने वाला रास्ता

terms.meaning: cell के कामों में सीधे energy देने वाला molecule
terms.image: काम चलाने के लिए तुरन्त खर्च किया जा सकने वाला छोटा energy token

why: The cell needs captured energy in usable ATP form.
Light-linked electron transport creates a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane.
Proton return through ATP synthase couples gradient dissipation to ATP formation.
items.example: Chloroplast → thylakoid membrane separating lumen from stroma.
items.leads_to: ATP joins NADPH as a light-reaction supply used by the Calvin cycle.
items.show: Accumulate H⁺ inside the lumen, then channel it through ATP synthase.
items.level_extra: Distinguish gradient formation from its controlled breakdown; ATP synthesis is coupled to the latter.

key_question.q: Why is an intact thylakoid membrane necessary?
key_question.a: It limits uncontrolled proton equilibration. A freely leaking membrane would dissipate the gradient without coupling its energy efficiently to ATP synthesis.

items.content: Splitting of water molecules is associated with PS II resulting in the release of O₂, protons and transfer of electrons to PS II.
items.exam_note: Water splitting belongs with PS II, not PS I; evolved O₂ comes from water.

terms.meaning: water से electrons निकालना, जिससे H⁺ और O₂ मिलते हैं
terms.image: एक source से तीन अलग outputs निकलना

why: PS II needs replacement electrons after electron donation.
Water splitting supplies electrons to PS II and releases protons and O₂.
Electron replacement permits continued light-driven transport.
items.example: The water-splitting system associated with PS II on the lumenal side of the thylakoid.
items.leads_to: Water contributes electrons, lumenal protons and the oxygen released by photosynthesis.
items.show: Split water into labelled electron, proton and oxygen outputs.
items.level_extra: The term photolysis is commonly used for water splitting; do not place the process at PS I.

key_question.q: Why is a replacement source of electrons needed?
key_question.a: A reaction centre that donates an electron must regain one to continue repeated charge separation. Water is the electron source for this photosynthetic flow.

items.content: In the carbon fixation cycle, CO₂ is added by the enzyme, RuBisCO, to a 5-carbon compound RuBP that is converted to 2 molecules of 3-carbon PGA. This is then converted to sugar by the Calvin cycle, and the RuBP is regenerated. During this process ATP and NADPH synthesised in the light reaction are utilised.
items.exam_note: Know acceptor, enzyme, first stable product, carbon counts, regeneration and energy/reducing-power inputs.

terms.meaning: CO₂ को RuBP से जोड़ने वाला enzyme, जो oxygenation भी कर सकता है
terms.image: जोड़ बनाने वाला worker जिसके पास दो तरह की reactions का विकल्प हो

terms.meaning: पाँच carbon वाला CO₂ लेने का molecule, जिसे cycle फिर बनाती है
terms.image: अगला सामान लेने के लिए बार-बार लौटती खाली tray

terms.meaning: CO₂ fixation के बाद मिलने वाला तीन carbon का compound
terms.image: छह मोतियों को दो तीन-तीन के हिस्सों में बाँटना

terms.meaning: इस्तेमाल के बाद फिर बन जाना ताकि अगला round चल सके
terms.image: काम के बाद tray फिर counter पर लौट आए

why: Incoming CO₂ needs an organic acceptor and its fixed carbon needs reduction.
RuBisCO-mediated fixation produces PGA, and ATP and NADPH support further conversion.
Regeneration of RuBP keeps the carbon fixation cycle running.
items.example: Leaf chloroplast stroma; trace one CO₂ into the Calvin cycle.
items.leads_to: Carbohydrate synthesis depends on both light-reaction supplies and continuous acceptor regeneration.
items.show: Join one carbon to five, split into two threes, and loop carbon back to RuBP.
items.level_extra: The cycle does not turn each PGA directly into one glucose molecule; show reduction, partial carbon exit and regeneration without implying complete export.
needs_first: ATP and NADPH from light reactions

key_question.q: How does the first fixation step conserve carbon atoms?
key_question.a: One carbon from CO₂ combines with the five-carbon acceptor, giving six carbons in total. The unstable six-carbon intermediate yields two three-carbon PGA molecules: 1 + 5 = 2 × 3.

items.content: RuBisCO also catalyses a wasteful oxygenation reaction in C₃ plants: photorespiration.
items.exam_note: RuBisCO is both carboxylase and oxygenase; photorespiration is not ordinary respiration.

terms.meaning: RuBisCO का RuBP के साथ CO₂ की जगह O₂ की reaction कराना
terms.image: सही input की जगह दूसरा input लगकर काम दूसरी दिशा में चला जाए

terms.meaning: light से जुड़ा वह pathway जिसमें oxygenation के बाद carbon और energy का नुकसान होता है
terms.image: factory में तैयार माल का कुछ हिस्सा वापस खो जाना

why: Efficient sugar production needs RuBisCO to fix CO₂.
RuBisCO can instead catalyse oxygenation in C₃ plants.
This route reduces net carbon gain and motivates a CO₂-concentrating solution.
items.example: C₃ leaf cells; oxygenation begins at RuBisCO in the chloroplast.
items.leads_to: The C₄ pathway can be introduced as a way to supply concentrated CO₂ to the Calvin cycle.
items.show: Branch RuBP towards CO₂ fixation or O₂-dependent carbon loss.
items.level_extra: C₃ denotes a three-carbon first stable fixation product; it does not count the number of cycle steps.

key_question.q: Why is RuBisCO not simply a beneficial CO₂-fixing enzyme in every reaction?
key_question.a: The page states that it also catalyses a wasteful oxygenation reaction in C₃ plants, called photorespiration.

items.content: Some tropical plants show a special type of photosynthesis called C₄ pathway. In these plants the first product of CO₂ fixation that takes place in the mesophyll, is a 4-carbon compound. In the bundle sheath cells the Calvin pathway is carried out for the synthesis of carbohydrates.
items.exam_note: C₄ initial fixation: mesophyll and four-carbon product; Calvin cycle: bundle sheath. C₄ plants still use the C₃ Calvin pathway.

terms.meaning: वह pathway जिसमें शुरुआती CO₂ fixation का पहला stable product चार carbon वाला होता है
terms.image: चार हिस्सों वाला carrier carbon को अगले काम की जगह तक ले जाए

terms.meaning: leaf की vascular bundles के चारों तरफ की cells
terms.image: बीच की pipe के चारों ओर लगी घेरती ring

why: RuBisCO benefits from an increased local CO₂ supply to limit oxygenation.
C₄ plants initially fix carbon into a four-carbon compound in mesophyll cells.
Carbon delivery to bundle sheath cells supports their Calvin cycle and suppresses photorespiration.
items.example: C₄ leaf → mesophyll initial fixation → bundle sheath Calvin cycle; maize is a standard example.
items.leads_to: Cell specialisation explains why a relatively small set of Calvin-cycle cells can support high productivity.
items.show: Move a four-carbon carrier from mesophyll to bundle sheath and release CO₂ beside RuBisCO.
items.level_extra: Name the trap: C₄ is an additional CO₂-concentrating route, not a replacement for the Calvin cycle. It also has an extra ATP cost.

key_question.q: Why is this spatial division useful?
key_question.a: Delivery and decarboxylation of four-carbon acids raise CO₂ around bundle sheath RuBisCO. This favours carboxylation and suppresses photorespiration.

items.content: EXERCISES
items.exam_note: Exercise heading.

items.content: 1. By looking at a plant externally can you tell whether a plant is C₃ or C₄? Why and how?
items.exam_note: Do not identify a pathway merely from a plant looking tropical or having a particular leaf shape.
needs_first: C₃ and C₄ first stable products

key_question.q: Why is an external visual guess insufficient?
key_question.a: The defining differences concern internal leaf organisation, cell-specific enzymes and carbon-fixation chemistry, not a universal visible feature of overall plant shape.

items.content: 2. By looking at which internal structure of a plant can you tell whether a plant is C₃ or C₄? Explain.
items.exam_note: Kranz means wreath-like arrangement; distinguish specialised Kranz anatomy from mere presence of a bundle sheath.

key_question.q: How does this arrangement support the C₄ mechanism?
key_question.a: Neighbouring mesophyll and bundle sheath cells provide sites for initial carbon fixation and the Calvin cycle, allowing four-carbon compounds to deliver CO₂ to bundle sheath RuBisCO.

items.content: 3. Even though a very few cells in a C₄ plant carry out the biosynthetic – Calvin pathway, yet they are highly productive. Can you discuss why?
items.exam_note: Explain the CO₂ pump and suppressed photorespiration; 'more cells' or 'no Calvin cycle' are incorrect explanations.

key_question.q: Why does concentrating CO₂ improve net carbon gain?
key_question.a: It favours RuBisCO carboxylation over oxygenation, so less previously fixed carbon and energy are lost through photorespiration.

items.content: 4. RuBisCO is an enzyme that acts both as a carboxylase and oxygenase. Why do you think RuBisCO carries out more carboxylation in C₄ plants?
items.exam_note: C₄ plants concentrate CO₂ near RuBisCO; they do not eliminate its capacity for oxygenation.

terms.meaning: CO₂ जोड़ने वाली reaction करवाने वाला enzyme
terms.image: काम की मेज पर CO₂ वाला packet जोड़ना।

terms.meaning: O₂ जोड़ने वाली reaction करवाने वाला enzyme
terms.image: उसी मेज पर दूसरा, O₂ वाला packet पहुँचना।

terms.meaning: RuBP की oxygenation के बाद बना compound सँभालने का रास्ता, जिसमें energy खर्च होती है और कुछ fixed carbon CO₂ बनकर निकलता है
terms.image: गलत बने सामान को सुधारने में मेहनत लगे और कुछ सामान भी खो जाए।

terms.meaning: leaf की vein के transport bundle को घेरने वाली cells की परत
terms.image: तारों के गुच्छे के चारों ओर लगी sleeve।

why: Carbon gain suffers when RuBisCO oxygenates RuBP and photorespiratory recovery loses carbon.
Mesophyll cells package captured carbon into four-carbon acids that deliver CO₂ to bundle sheath cells.
CO₂ released beside RuBisCO favours carboxylation and suppresses oxygenation.
items.example: A maize leaf: trace carbon from mesophyll into the bundle sheath surrounding a vein.
items.leads_to: The C₄ delivery mechanism reduces photorespiratory loss while retaining the Calvin cycle.
items.show: Pack carbon, deliver it inward, release CO₂, and contrast CO₂ versus O₂ addition to RuBP.
items.level_extra: Distinguish photorespiration from mitochondrial respiration and CO₂ concentration from an altered RuBisCO.
needs_first: RuBP as the Calvin-cycle CO₂ acceptor

key_question.q: Why is oxygenation a disadvantage for carbon gain?
key_question.a: The two-carbon phosphoglycolate must be processed through the photorespiratory pathway. This recovery process consumes energy and releases some previously fixed carbon as CO₂ without producing sugar. Photorespiration therefore reduces the efficiency of photosynthetic carbon gain; it is not another name for ordinary mitochondrial respiration.

items.content: 5. Suppose there were plants that had a high concentration of Chlorophyll b, but lacked chlorophyll a, would it carry out photosynthesis? Then why do plants have chlorophyll b and other accessory pigments?
items.exam_note: Separate light harvesting from photochemical electron transfer; chlorophyll a occurs in both antenna and reaction centres.

terms.meaning: thylakoid membrane में pigments और proteins की मिलकर काम करने वाली unit
terms.image: कई collectors और एक काम शुरू करने वाला centre, एक ही टीम में।

terms.meaning: रोशनी पकड़कर उसकी energy reaction centre तक पहुँचाने वाले pigments का समूह
terms.image: कई लोग सामान इकट्ठा करके एक काम की मेज तक पहुँचाते हैं।

terms.meaning: वह हिस्सा जहाँ excited chlorophyll a से electron निकलकर acceptor तक जाता है
terms.image: सामान इकट्ठा करने की जगह से अलग, वह मेज जहाँ असली काम शुरू होता है।

terms.meaning: रोशनी मिलने पर pigment में आई अतिरिक्त energy
terms.image: झूले को धक्का देने पर वह ऊँचा उठता है; pigment की energy भी बढ़ती है।

terms.meaning: electron देने वाला हिस्सा और electron लेने वाला हिस्सा अलग charges वाले हो जाते हैं
terms.image: एक जगह से सिक्का दूसरी जगह गया: पहली जगह कमी, दूसरी जगह बढ़त।

terms.meaning: chlorophyll a की मदद के लिए अलग wavelengths की रोशनी पकड़ने वाले pigments
terms.image: अलग आकार की छलनियाँ अलग चीज़ें पकड़ती हैं; pigments अलग रंगों की रोशनी पकड़ते हैं।

why: A plant needs both effective light collection and a way to turn that excitation into electron transfer.
Antenna pigments broaden light capture and funnel excitation toward reaction-centre chlorophyll a.
Without that chlorophyll a centre, more chlorophyll b supplies collection capacity but cannot restore the missing photochemical step.
items.example: Zoom from a green leaf to a chloroplast, then to a photosystem embedded in its thylakoid membrane.
items.leads_to: Accessory pigments complement chlorophyll a rather than replace its reaction-centre function.
items.show: Collect light across an antenna, funnel excitation inward, then transfer an electron to an acceptor.
items.level_extra: NEET trap: energy transfer through antenna pigments is distinct from reaction-centre electron transfer; chlorophyll a is also an antenna pigment.

key_question.q: What do excitation energy and charge separation mean here?
key_question.a: Absorbing light raises a pigment to a higher-energy, or excited, state. Antenna pigments pass this excitation energy toward the reaction centre; this is not the same as passing one electron through the entire antenna. At the reaction centre, excited chlorophyll a donates an electron to an acceptor, leaving positive and negative charges separated. This starts photochemical electron transfer.

items.content: 6. Why is the colour of a leaf kept in the dark frequently yellow, or pale green? Which pigment do you think is more stable?
items.exam_note: Xanthophylls are yellow carotenoids; pigment unmasking is not conversion of chlorophyll into carotenoids.

terms.meaning: chlorophyll की मदद करने वाले pigments का समूह, जिसमें पीले xanthophylls और पीले-नारंगी carotenes आते हैं
terms.image: हरे रंग के साथ मौजूद पीले और नारंगी रंग।

terms.meaning: carotenoids में आने वाले पीले pigments
terms.image: हरे cover के पीछे पहले से मौजूद पीली sheet।

terms.meaning: एक pigment का रंग इतना उभरना कि दूसरे का रंग साफ न दिखे
terms.image: पीली sheet को ढकता हरा cover; यह रंग समझाने की मिसाल है।

why: A green leaf may contain yellow pigments whose colour is concealed by chlorophyll's dominance.
In prolonged darkness chlorophyll replenishment is impaired and chlorophyll can decline.
The relatively persistent yellow pigments become visible; remaining chlorophyll can instead give pale green.
items.example: Compare a green leaf before and after prolonged darkness.
items.leads_to: The colour change reveals relative pigment persistence rather than newly formed yellow pigment.
items.show: Fade green to reveal an already-present yellow contribution.
items.level_extra: Distinguish complete darkness from shade acclimation in question 7.

key_question.q: Why can prolonged darkness make the leaf yellow or pale green?
key_question.a: Prolonged darkness impairs chlorophyll replenishment and can lead to chlorophyll loss. As its green contribution weakens, persistent yellow carotenoids, especially xanthophylls, become visible. If appreciable chlorophyll remains, the leaf may appear pale green rather than yellow.

items.content: 7. Look at leaves of the same plant on the shady side and compare it with the leaves on the sunny side. Or, compare the potted plants kept in the sunlight with those in the shade. Which of them has leaves that are darker green ? Why?
items.exam_note: Lower a:b means relatively more b; shade is not darkness, and darker colour does not establish a greater photosynthetic rate.

terms.meaning: कम रोशनी के हिसाब से plant का अपना काम और बनावट ढालना
terms.image: कम रोशनी में पढ़ने के लिए किताब की जगह बदलकर उपलब्ध उजाला लेना।

terms.meaning: pigments और proteins की टोली जो रोशनी पकड़कर energy reaction centre तक पहुँचाती है
terms.image: कई collectors एक काम की मेज तक सामान पहुँचाते हैं।

terms.meaning: chlorophyll a की मात्रा को b की मात्रा से तुलना करके बताना
terms.image: तीन हरे tokens के साथ एक की जगह दो दूसरे tokens हों तो उनका आपसी अनुपात बदलता है।

why: Shade supplies fewer photons, creating a need to capture available light effectively.
Leaves can adjust their antenna investment and pigment composition, commonly increasing chlorophyll relative to tissue mass and b relative to a.
Greater pigment investment can make shade leaves appear darker without implying a higher photosynthetic rate.
items.example: Compare healthy shaded and sun-exposed leaves on the same plant.
items.leads_to: Shade adjustment and prolonged-darkness yellowing are different responses.
items.show: Reduce incoming photons, enlarge the collecting antenna, and compare a and b token groups.
items.level_extra: A ratio reports relative composition, not absolute pigment amount.

key_question.q: How do these adjustments help explain darker shade leaves?
key_question.a: With fewer incoming photons, investment in light-harvesting pigments helps intercept available light. Shade leaves commonly have more chlorophyll relative to tissue mass and relatively more chlorophyll b in antenna complexes. Greater pigment investment can give a darker-green appearance; the lower a:b ratio indicates antenna adjustment rather than independently proving a darker colour or a higher photosynthetic rate.

items.content: 8. Figure 11.10 shows the effect of light on the rate of photosynthesis. Based on the graph, answer the following questions:
items.exam_note: The referenced figure is needed to verify letter-specific answers.
needs_first: reading axes and slopes on a graph

items.content: (a) At which point/s (A, B or C) in the curve is light a limiting factor?
items.exam_note: Use the response to increased light, not the absolute rate; letter assignments require the missing figure.

terms.meaning: जिस जरूरत की कमी इस समय rate को आगे बढ़ने से रोक रही है
terms.image: सबसे धीमे counter पर अटकी पूरी queue।

terms.meaning: light में बदलाव पर rate कितना बदलता है, इसका माप
terms.image: दाईं ओर चलते हुए रास्ता कितना ऊपर चढ़ता है।

terms.meaning: इतनी light मिलना कि और light बढ़ाने पर rate खास न बढ़े
terms.image: काम की मेज भर चुकी हो तो और सामान भेजने से काम तेज न होना।

why: A low rate alone does not identify which requirement is insufficient.
Increase light with other conditions fixed and observe the vertical change in rate.
A rise shows light responsiveness; a plateau directs attention to other constraints.
items.example: Illustrative arbitrary-unit comparison only: light 10→20, rate 2→4; at saturation light 40→50, rate 6→6.
items.leads_to: The curve's response identifies light limitation without guessing missing labels.
items.show: Move right along the light axis, rise with the curve, then flatten into a plateau.
items.level_extra: These illustrative numbers do not reconstruct Figure 11.10.
needs_first: changing one experimental condition while holding others fixed

key_question.q: Can a small example make this test concrete without reconstructing Figure 11.10?
key_question.a: Purely illustrative values in arbitrary units: if light increases from 10 to 20 and rate rises from 2 to 4 while other conditions remain fixed, the response shows light limitation in that interval. If a further light increase from 40 to 50 leaves rate at 6, that interval is light-saturated. These invented teaching values are not observations or letter positions from the missing figure.

items.content: (b) What could be the limiting factor/s in region A?
items.exam_note: A plateau is not cessation of photosynthesis; water shortage often acts through stomatal closure and restricted CO₂ supply.

terms.meaning: leaf की reactions एक समय में जितना काम कर सकती हैं
terms.image: बिजली पूरी है, पर कुछ ही रसोइये खाना बना सकते हैं।

terms.meaning: leaf की बाहरी परत के छोटे pores जिनसे CO₂ अंदर और water vapour बाहर जा सकती है
terms.image: दरवाजा छोटा बंद हो तो अंदर आने वाला सामान भी कम हो जाए।

why: Even with abundant light, carbon fixation needs CO₂ and functioning enzymes.
Finite enzyme activity or restricted CO₂ entry can become the bottleneck; water shortage can close stomata and reduce that entry.
Adding light cannot remove this bottleneck, so test another requirement while holding light fixed.
items.example: A water-stressed leaf with partly closed stomata under strong sunlight.
items.leads_to: A light-saturated rate can rise only if a relevant non-light constraint is relieved.
items.show: Narrow a leaf pore, reduce entering CO₂ particles, and hold the light beam constant.
items.level_extra: Interpret A as a plateau only after checking Figure 11.10; temperature increases do not improve rate indefinitely.
needs_first: CO₂ as a substrate for carbon fixation

key_question.q: How can water shortage restrict CO₂ fixation even when light is abundant?
key_question.a: Stomata are small pores in the leaf epidermis whose opening is regulated by guard cells. CO₂ enters through these pores, while water vapour can escape. Water shortage promotes stomatal closure to conserve water; narrower pores reduce CO₂ entry, decreasing the carbon supply for fixation. This is the chain water shortage → pore closure → reduced CO₂ entry → restricted photosynthesis.

items.content: (c) What do C and D represent on the curve?
items.exam_note: Zero net exchange at compensation is not zero gross photosynthesis; at zero light, negative net uptake indicates respiration.

terms.meaning: respiration में निकलने वाला CO₂ घटाने से पहले photosynthesis में fix हुआ पूरा CO₂
terms.image: खर्च घटाने से पहले मिली पूरी रकम।

terms.meaning: photosynthesis में लिया CO₂ और respiration में छोड़ा CO₂, इनका बचा हुआ balance
terms.image: आमदनी में से खर्च घटाकर बची रकम।

terms.meaning: वह light intensity जहाँ CO₂ fixation और respiratory release बराबर हों
terms.image: दो बराबर पलड़ों वाला तराजू; दोनों तरफ चीजें हैं, पर balance शून्य है।

terms.meaning: अँधेरे में भी जारी रहने वाली respiration से CO₂ निकलना
terms.image: आमदनी रुकी हो, फिर भी जरूरी खर्च चलता रहे।

why: A gas-exchange measurement combines CO₂ uptake and release, so zero exchange needs explanation.
Equal gross fixation and respiratory release cancel in the net balance even though both occur.
At zero light, fixation is absent but respiration can continue, producing negative net uptake.
items.example: Illustrative rates: fixation 2 minus respiration 2 gives 0 at compensation; in darkness 0 minus 2 gives −2.
items.leads_to: A zero crossing and a negative dark intercept represent different physiological conditions.
items.show: Balance inward and outward CO₂ arrows, then remove the inward arrow at zero light.
items.level_extra: The illustrative balance explains graph features but does not establish the missing C/D label assignments.

key_question.q: How does a numerical balance explain the light compensation point?
key_question.a: Use purely illustrative rates in μmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹, meaning micromoles of CO₂ per square metre of leaf per second. If gross fixation is 2 and respiratory release is 2, net uptake is 2−2=0. The light intensity producing this balance is the light compensation point. If added light raises gross fixation to 5 while release remains 2 in this example, net uptake becomes 3. These numbers are teaching examples, not data from Figure 11.10.

items.content: 9. Give comparison between the following:
items.exam_note: The three comparisons are captured separately below.

items.content: (a) C₃ and C₄ pathways
items.exam_note: Distinguish acceptor carbon count from first-product carbon count; compare enzymes, locations, energy cost and photorespiration.

terms.meaning: पहले से मौजूद molecule जो आने वाला carbon पकड़ता है
terms.image: आए हुए सामान को रखने वाली खाली ट्रे।

terms.meaning: ribulose bisphosphate: पाँच carbon वाला sugar, जिस पर दो phosphate groups हैं; Calvin cycle का CO₂ acceptor
terms.image: पाँच खाने वाली ट्रे पर एक नया carbon आता है, फिर बनी चीज़ दो हिस्सों में बँटती है।

terms.meaning: phosphoenolpyruvate: तीन carbon वाला molecule, जो C₄ की शुरुआती fixation में carbon लेता है
terms.image: तीन जुड़े डिब्बों में एक डिब्बा और जोड़ना।

terms.meaning: oxaloacetic acid: C₄ fixation का पहला टिकने वाला चार-carbon product
terms.image: तीन डिब्बों में एक जुड़ा, अब चार का समूह बना।

terms.meaning: 3-phosphoglyceric acid: Calvin cycle में fixation के बाद मिलने वाला तीन-carbon product
terms.image: छह टुकड़ों का समूह टूटकर तीन-तीन के दो समूह बनता है।

terms.meaning: adenosine triphosphate: reactions चलाने के लिए इस्तेमाल होने वाली energy देने वाला molecule
terms.image: काम में खर्च होने और फिर charge होने वाला energy token।

terms.meaning: reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate: carbon को carbohydrate की ओर बदलने के लिए electrons पहुँचाने वाला carrier
terms.image: ज़रूरी सामान लेकर पहुँची हुई delivery गाड़ी।

why: Incoming carbon must be captured before it can be built into carbohydrate; distinguish the receiver, catalyst and resulting product.
C₃ fixation feeds the Calvin cycle directly, whereas initial C₄ fixation packages carbon into four-carbon acids for delivery near RuBisCO.
Delivery raises local CO₂ and reduces photorespiration, but regenerating the initial PEP acceptor costs extra ATP.
items.example: Compare a wheat leaf with a maize leaf: trace carbon from initial capture to the chloroplast where the Calvin cycle operates.
items.leads_to: C₄ is a CO₂-concentrating addition to, not a replacement for, the Calvin cycle.
items.show: Receive carbon, label the catalyst, count product carbons, then deliver carbon to the Calvin cycle.
items.level_extra: NEET: C₃ acceptor has five carbons; C₄ acceptor has three. Initial C₄ fixation uses PEP carboxylase, but its Calvin cycle still uses RuBisCO.

key_question.q: Why is C₄ not an alternative that eliminates the Calvin cycle?
key_question.a: The initial C₄ reactions act like a carbon delivery and concentration system. After delivery, CO₂ still enters the Calvin cycle through RuBisCO and produces 3-PGA. C₄ plants therefore use the Calvin cycle as well as their preliminary four-carbon pathway.

items.content: (b) Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
items.exam_note: Cyclic: PSI and ATP, no net NADPH or O₂. Non-cyclic: PSII then PSI, ATP, NADPH and O₂. H⁺ return is lumen to stroma.

terms.meaning: रोशनी से चलने वाली प्रक्रिया के सहारे ADP में phosphate जोड़कर ATP बनाना
terms.image: धूप से मिली energy से rechargeable token दोबारा तैयार करना।

terms.meaning: रोशनी पकड़कर electron transfer शुरू करने वाली दो photosystem units; इनके centres P700 और P680 हैं
terms.image: एक रास्ते पर दो energy देने वाले पड़ाव; non-cyclic flow में II पहले आता है।

terms.meaning: stroma thylakoid के बाहर का fluid है; lumen thylakoid की थैली के अंदर की जगह है
terms.image: पानी में रखी बंद थैली: बाहर का पानी और थैली के अंदर की जगह अलग हैं।

terms.meaning: membrane के दोनों ओर H⁺ की मात्रा और charge में ऐसा फर्क जिसमें energy जमा है
terms.image: बाँध के दोनों ओर पानी का अलग स्तर।

terms.meaning: membrane में लगी protein machine जो H⁺ के बहाव से ATP बनाती है
terms.image: पानी के बहाव से घूमकर काम करने वाली turbine।

terms.meaning: grana के thylakoid stacks को जोड़ने वाली बिना stack की membrane
terms.image: सिक्कों के दो ढेरों को जोड़ता पतला पुल।

why: The chloroplast needs ATP, so light energy must be converted into a form that ATP-making machinery can use.
Electron transport builds a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, storing energy like water held behind a barrier.
Protons return through ATP synthase to power ATP production; cyclic flow builds this energy store without net NADPH formation.
items.example: Zoom into a chloroplast: mark stroma outside a thylakoid, lumen inside it, and ATP synthase spanning the boundary.
items.leads_to: Both electron routes can support ATP synthesis, but only non-cyclic flow supplies net NADPH and releases O₂.
items.show: Trace a loop versus a through-route, accumulate H⁺ in the lumen, then let H⁺ return through ATP synthase.
items.level_extra: NEET traps: PSI numbering does not indicate the first step; cyclic flow does not split water; ATP synthesis is driven by H⁺ return into the stroma.

key_question.q: Why can cyclic flow make ATP even though its electrons return?
key_question.a: The electron circuit can drive proton movement and build the gradient before the electrons return to PSI. The gradient, not the mere return of an electron to chlorophyll, powers ATP synthase. Cyclic flow can therefore supplement ATP without also producing NADPH.

items.content: (c) Anatomy of leaf in C₃ and C₄ plants
items.exam_note: Kranz anatomy combines large chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells, thick walls and no intercellular spaces; connect spatial arrangement to CO₂ concentration.

terms.meaning: leaf की vein के अंदर xylem और phloem का साथ लगा transport समूह
terms.image: एक ही रास्ते में साथ रखी पानी की पाइप और सामान ले जाने की लाइन।

terms.meaning: vascular bundle के चारों ओर लगी cells की घेरने वाली परत
terms.image: तारों के गुच्छे के चारों ओर चढ़ी sleeve।

terms.meaning: leaf की ऊपर और नीचे की epidermis के बीच का photosynthesis करने वाला tissue
terms.image: sandwich की दोनों बाहरी परतों के बीच की भराई; इसमें veins भी गुजरती हैं।

terms.meaning: vascular bundle के चारों ओर बड़ी bundle sheath cells और बाहर mesophyll की खास wreath-जैसी बनावट

why: C₄ photosynthesis needs to deliver captured carbon to a protected site near RuBisCO.
Mesophyll surrounds the bundle sheath, allowing four-carbon compounds to reach neighbouring sheath cells and release CO₂ there.
The chloroplast-rich sheath and restricted gas escape help maintain local CO₂, linking Kranz structure to reduced photorespiration.

items.leads_to: An anatomical arrangement enables cooperation between two cell types; C₃ leaves should not be described as lacking bundle sheaths altogether.
items.show: Cut across a vein, reveal nested tissues, and move four-carbon compounds from mesophyll into the sheath.
items.level_extra: NEET: identify Kranz anatomy from spatial arrangement and bundle sheath features; avoid universal claims about grana or palisade–spongy differentiation.

key_question.q: How does the spatial arrangement support carbon delivery?
key_question.a: Mesophyll cells initially fix carbon into four-carbon compounds, which are transferred to nearby bundle sheath cells. Decarboxylation there releases CO₂ close to RuBisCO. The close arrangement supports transfer, while restricted outward diffusion helps retain CO₂, favouring carboxylation and suppressing photorespiration.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis in plant physiology and the living world
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Plant physiology connects molecular and cellular events with whole-plant function and environmental conditions, complementing the organismic perspective associated with ecology. Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process using light energy to synthesise organic food; the chapter contrasts autotrophic plants with dependent heterotrophs and emphasises food supply and atmospheric oxygen, with CO₂ entering leaves through stomata.

concepts.name: Experimental requirements: chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Starch formation in illuminated green regions, compared with non-green or black-paper-covered regions, provides evidence for chlorophyll and light requirements. KOH removes CO₂ from the enclosed portion of a leaf; its failure to accumulate starch while the air-exposed portion does so supports the requirement for CO₂ through a controlled comparison.

concepts.name: Priestley and Ingenhousz: restoration of air and oxygen release
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Priestley's 1770 bell-jar comparisons suggested that plants restore what burning candles and breathing animals remove from air; the figure has two separate before–after sequences, with and without a plant, and oxygen was identified by Priestley in 1774. Ingenhousz's light–dark comparisons and oxygen bubbles around illuminated green aquatic-plant parts established the roles of sunlight and green tissues; the rekindling question tests how to examine restored air without opening the setup.

concepts.name: Sachs and Engelmann: carbohydrate production and action spectrum
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Around 1854, Sachs linked green chloroplast-containing parts with glucose production and storage as starch. Engelmann illuminated Cladophora with prism-separated light and used aerobic-bacterial accumulation to detect oxygen evolution, obtaining an early action spectrum with strong blue and red responses; together such work established light-driven carbohydrate formation from CO₂ and water.

concepts.name: Hydrogen donors, oxygen source and overall equations
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. The empirical CO₂ + H₂O → [CH₂O] + O₂ equation is expanded by van Niel's donor generalisation, 2H₂A + CO₂ → 2A + CH₂O + H₂O: water is the donor in green plants, whereas H₂S-using bacteria produce sulphur or sulphate rather than oxygen. The overall plant equation is 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ in light, describing many reactions rather than one; retaining substrate and product water makes the water-derived oxygen accounting explicit.

concepts.name: Chloroplast location, structure and division of labour
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Photosynthesis occurs in leaves and other green parts; mesophyll chloroplasts position themselves along cell walls to obtain suitable incident light, and the orientation question asks students to reason about their flat surfaces and light direction. Identify the outer and inner envelope membranes, grana, connecting stromal lamellae, stroma, ribosomes, starch granules and lipid droplets: membranes carry light trapping and ATP/NADPH formation, whereas stromal enzyme reactions synthesise sugars, so 'dark reaction' means indirect rather than absent light dependence.

concepts.name: Leaf pigments and their chromatographic colours
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Paper chromatography reveals chlorophyll a, bright or blue-green; chlorophyll b, yellow-green; xanthophylls, yellow; and carotenoids, yellow to yellow-orange, showing that leaf colour comes from a pigment mixture. Pigments absorb particular wavelengths; the abundance, dark-leaf yellowing and shade-versus-sun questions should be distinguished from these directly stated observations, and explanations of pigment stability or shade acclimation require an outside basis.

concepts.name: Absorption spectra, action spectra and accessory-pigment functions
concepts.explanation: Basis: book and supplied figure descriptions. Absorption spectra plot pigment absorption against wavelength, whereas the action spectrum plots photosynthetic rate measured by O₂ release: chlorophyll a has prominent blue and red peaks, chlorophyll b has shifted peaks, and carotenoids absorb mainly blue light. The spectra correspond but do not overlap completely: chlorophyll a is the chief pigment, while accessory pigments transfer absorbed energy to it, widen usable wavelengths and protect it from photo-oxidation; intermediate-wavelength photosynthesis is not zero, and the superimposed curves do not share a numerical rate–absorption scale.

concepts.name: Light-harvesting complexes and reaction centres
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. The photochemical phase includes absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and ATP/NADPH formation; hundreds of protein-bound antenna pigments funnel photon energy to the reaction-centre chlorophyll a, which transfers an excited electron to a primary acceptor. PS I contains P700 and PS II contains P680, named for absorption maxima of 700 and 680 nm; photosystem numbering follows discovery, not functional order.

concepts.name: Non-cyclic electron transport and the Z scheme
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Light excites P680 electrons to an acceptor; carriers pass them downhill to PS I, where light excites electrons again and a second acceptor pathway ultimately reduces NADP⁺ to NADPH. Electrons are transferred rather than used up, and the two light-driven rises and intervening descents produce the Z-shaped arrangement on a redox-potential scale; non-cyclic flow operates PS II then PS I and supports ATP and NADPH formation.

concepts.name: Water splitting supplies replacement electrons
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Electrons lost from PS II are replaced by its associated water-splitting complex, while PS II supplies replacement electrons to PS I through the transport chain. The reaction 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ releases protons on the lumen-facing side of the thylakoid membrane and establishes water as the source of evolved oxygen.

concepts.name: Cyclic versus non-cyclic photophosphorylation
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Photophosphorylation forms ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light; in cyclic flow, excited PS I electrons return through carriers to P700 instead of reducing NADP⁺, producing ATP without NADPH. Contrast this with the PS II-to-PS I non-cyclic pathway; the book identifies stromal lamellae lacking PS II and NADP reductase as a possible cyclic-flow location and also associates cyclic flow with excitation wavelengths beyond 680 nm.

concepts.name: Chemiosmosis: proton gradient and ATP synthase
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Water oxidation adds lumen protons, hydrogen-carrier transport moves protons from stroma to lumen, and stromal NADP⁺ reduction removes stromal protons, producing high lumen H⁺, lower lumen pH and an electrochemical gradient. In the figure, follow PS II → PQ/PQH₂ → cytochrome B6f → PC → PS I → Fd → FNR, separately from proton movement; proton return through membrane CF₀ drives conformational changes in stromal CF₁ and ATP synthesis, requiring a membrane, proton pump, gradient and ATP synthase.

concepts.name: Calvin's investigation and indirect light dependence of biosynthesis
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Light-reaction oxygen diffuses out, while ATP and NADPH drive stromal sugar synthesis; biosynthesis briefly continues after light removal and then stops, demonstrating indirect light dependence rather than a requirement for darkness. Calvin, born in Minnesota in April 1911, earned his chemistry Ph.D. there and worked at Berkeley; his post-war work with Bassham using ¹⁴CO₂ identified three-carbon PGA and mapped carbon assimilation, earning the 1961 Nobel Prize, while his electron-transfer ideas and photosynthetic principles connect to solar-energy and renewable-resource research.

concepts.name: C₃ and C₄ classification and the unexpected RuBP acceptor
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. C₃ plants have three-carbon PGA as the first stable fixation product, whereas C₄ plants initially form four-carbon OAA; this classification concerns the initial stable product, not whether the Calvin cycle exists. The Calvin-cycle acceptor is five-carbon ketose RuBP, not the initially suspected two-carbon compound, and its regeneration makes a cycle shared by photosynthetic plants including C₄ plants.

concepts.name: Calvin-cycle stages and carbon flow
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Carboxylation uses RuBisCO to combine CO₂ with RuBP and form two 3-PGA molecules; reduction uses ATP and NADPH to produce carbohydrate intermediates, and regeneration uses ATP to restore RuBP. Trace the figure's triose-phosphate branch toward sucrose and starch separately from its return to RuBP, and distinguish the two ATP plus two NADPH used in reduction per CO₂ from the additional ATP used in regeneration.

concepts.name: Calvin-cycle energy budget and supplementary cyclic ATP
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Each CO₂ fixed requires three ATP and two NADPH; six turns fix six CO₂ to produce the glucose-equivalent output, consuming eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH and returning eighteen ADP and twelve oxidised NADP carriers. The book proposes that cyclic phosphorylation probably helps meet the unequal ATP and NADPH requirements; teach this as its suggested explanation, not a demonstrated fixed coupling ratio.

concepts.name: C₄ adaptations and Kranz anatomy
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. C₄ plants adapted to dry tropical conditions have distinctive anatomy, high-light and higher-temperature responses, greater biomass productivity and, in the chapter's account, no photorespiration. Kranz means wreath: large chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells surround vascular bundles, may form several layers, have thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and lack intercellular spaces; compare vertical sections, including maize or sorghum, rather than relying on external appearance.

concepts.name: Hatch and Slack pathway and cellular compartmentation
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. In C₄ mesophyll cells, three-carbon PEP accepts inorganic carbon through PEPcase to form OAA, followed by malic or aspartic acid; C₄ acids move to bundle sheath cells, release CO₂ for the Calvin cycle, and return a three-carbon compound for PEP regeneration. The figure shows bicarbonate input, cell boundaries and plasmodesmatal transport; distinguish PEPcase-containing mesophyll lacking RuBisCO from RuBisCO-rich bundle sheath lacking PEPcase, whereas C₃ Calvin fixation occurs in mesophyll.

concepts.name: RuBisCO competition, photorespiration and C₄ productivity
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. RuBisCO, described as the most abundant enzyme, competitively binds CO₂ or O₂; normal RuBP carboxylation yields two PGA molecules, whereas oxygenation yields one phosphoglycerate and a two-carbon phosphoglycolate, reducing carbon fixation. Photorespiration consumes ATP and releases CO₂ without producing sugars, ATP or NADPH; C₄-acid decarboxylation raises bundle sheath CO₂ around RuBisCO, minimises oxygenase activity and explains the chapter's absence of C₄ photorespiration and higher productivity.

concepts.name: Integrated C₃–C₄ comparison and table practice
concepts.explanation: Basis: book, with table entries requiring student inference from the chapter. Complete all seventeen characteristics: Calvin and initial-fixation locations, number of fixing cell types, primary acceptors and carbon counts, first products and carbon counts, RuBisCO and PEPcase, RuBisCO location, high-light fixation, photorespiration under low/high light and low/high CO₂, temperature optima and observed examples. Preserve the printed choices: mesophyll/bundle sheath/both; the one-, two- or three-cell-type alternatives; RuBP/PEP/PGA; acceptor counts 5/4/3; PGA/OAA/RuBP/PEP; product counts 3/4/5; Yes/No/Not always; mesophyll/bundle sheath/none; Low/high/medium; High/negligible/sometimes; and 30–40°C/20–25°C/above 40°C, with examples investigated through leaf sections.

concepts.name: Internal and external factors and Blackman's law
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Internal controls include leaf number, size, age and orientation, mesophyll and chloroplast characteristics, internal CO₂ and chlorophyll, linked to genetic predisposition and growth; external controls include light, temperature, CO₂ and water. Blackman's 1905 law identifies the factor nearest its minimum as the one whose change directly changes rate, explaining why optimal light and CO₂ cannot overcome very low temperature.

concepts.name: Light response, saturation and graph interpretation
concepts.explanation: Basis: book and supplied figure description. Distinguish light quality, intensity and duration: fixation rises approximately linearly at low intensity, bends as other factors limit it, and reaches a plateau; the book states saturation around ten per cent of full sunlight and warns that sufficiently excessive light breaks down chlorophyll and decreases photosynthesis. In Figure 11.10, A marks the rising region, B the transition and C the plateau; D projects saturation-region intensity onto the horizontal axis and E projects plateau rate onto the vertical axis, so answer the exercise from those actual labels.

concepts.name: CO₂ concentration and greenhouse enrichment
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. The text gives atmospheric CO₂ as 0.03–0.04%, describes stimulation up to 0.05% with possible long-term damage beyond it, and identifies CO₂ as a major limiting factor; these are the book's values rather than a claim about present measurements. Neither C₃ nor C₄ plants responds to added CO₂ under low light, whereas under high light C₄ saturation occurs near 360 µL L⁻¹ and C₃ saturation beyond 450 µL L⁻¹, explaining CO₂-enriched greenhouse production of tomatoes and bell pepper.

concepts.name: Temperature, habitat and indirect water-stress effects
concepts.explanation: Basis: book. Enzymatic carbon reactions are strongly temperature-controlled, while light reactions are less temperature-sensitive; C₄ plants have higher temperature optima than C₃ plants, and tropical plants higher optima than temperate-adapted plants. Water affects photosynthesis chiefly through plant condition: stress closes stomata and restricts CO₂, while wilting reduces leaf surface area and metabolic activity, rather than acting simply through a shortage of photolysis substrate.

prerequisites.name: Plant cells, leaf tissues and stomatal gas exchange

prerequisites.name: Chemical formulae, balanced equations and carbon conservation
prerequisites.why: Distinguish coefficients from subscripts, interpret H⁺ and e⁻, balance water and oxygen, and count carbons through acceptors and products.

prerequisites.name: Oxidation, reduction and electron transfer
prerequisites.why: Understand hydrogen donors, electron excitation and transfer, water oxidation, carrier reduction and NADP⁺ conversion.

prerequisites.name: ATP–ADP phosphate transfer and NADP⁺–NADPH reducing power
prerequisites.why: Separate energy supply from reducing power and interpret photophosphorylation, biosynthesis and quantitative carrier budgets.

prerequisites.name: Enzyme catalysis, active sites and competing substrates
prerequisites.why: Explain RuBisCO and PEPcase, temperature-sensitive carbon reactions and competitive CO₂/O₂ binding.

prerequisites.name: Membrane compartments, proton gradients, diffusion and pH
prerequisites.why: Distinguish lumen from stroma, follow proton accumulation and return, and connect greater H⁺ concentration with lower pH.

prerequisites.name: Visible-light wavelength and quantitative graph reading
prerequisites.why: Interpret wavelength colours, absorption versus rate, approximate peaks, curve slopes, plateaus, axis projections, percentages and concentration units.

prerequisites.name: Controlled comparisons, starch evidence and isotope tracing
prerequisites.why: Infer requirements from matched leaf or jar conditions, use starch as evidence of carbohydrate formation, and understand how labelled carbon reveals reaction intermediates.
